speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF MALAYSIA AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and my pleasure to welcome to our House of Commons Tunku Abdul Rahman, the prime minister of Malaysia, together with two members of his government, the ambassador in Washington, minister without portfolio, and the minister of information and broadcasting, and other members of their party. The prime minister was last here in 1960 as the prime minister of Malaya. We now welcome him as the prime minister of Malaysia, the federation of Malaya, Singapore, Sarawak and Sabah. This imaginative concept was largely his. Indeed, I believe he can consider himself as the major founder of the new federation. Under his leadership the peoples of Malaysia have been brought closer together in freedom, democracy and greater human welfare.
Today, Mr. Speaker, as we know, they are resisting political, economic and indeed military pressure from outside; pressure dedicated to their destruction. In the words of the communique of the recent commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London, we give the prime minister and his people the assurance of our sympathy and, perhaps what is more important, our support in their resistance to this kind of aggression. We are happy indeed that Malaysia is in the commonwealth of nations. We are proud to be associated with her in that great association that spans the world. Our two countries have always enjoyed friendly relations, and these relations will be even closer as a result of this visit which, though very short, will I hope be a happy and fruitful one.
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, from time to time there are instances in the house of complete agreement. This is one of those occasions. I join with the Prime Minister in welcoming the prime minister of Malaysia, Tunku Rahman, an outstanding statesman, a wise counsellor and one who, by reason of his
membership in the British bar, has applied the principles of the rule of law and parliamentary government in his country. His enlightened leadership deserves the commendation of all who cherish freedom.
The Prime Minister has said in effect that throughout his life the Tunku has been in the front line of freedom. No one among the leaders of the various countries of the world has been a more dedicated fighter in the cause of freedom against communists. The Prime Minister has said in effect that the Tunku was the architect of unity in his country. He has now become the father of Malaysia, dedicated to the commonwealth. He was present at those prime ministers' conferences of 1960 and 1961 when we laid the foundations of non-discrimination on the basis of colour, race or creed within this commonwealth, consummated as were those concepts at the last meeting of the prime ministers.
The eyes of Asia are upon the Federation of Malaysia. The state of Malaya, as it was, was subject to a ceaseless barrage of propaganda, infiltration and subversion from red China. Against such activities, under his sterling stand for freedom Malaya was triumphant. Today, as the Prime Minister says, the federation faces other challenges; indeed, faces survival from overt aggression.
I was glad when the prime ministers' conference came out not only with words of sympathy but of promised support for Malaysia. Experience has shown that sympathy or moral support is not much of a rampart against aggression. Anything that the government of Canada may do, already having given certain undertakings for the training of forces within our country, the provision of technicians and also, I would say, additional credit for other requirements by Malaysia, will receive the support of the Canadian people as a whole.
I join with the Prime Minister in his words of official welcome. I join too as one who is honoured to number the Tunku among his friends. I visited Malaya; I visited Singapore. In both those places I received that reception that is characteristic of the commonwealth. Today in giving this welcome to a great leader in the commonwealth, a

The members of this party are happy to join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in extending a hearty welcome to His Royal Highness Tunku Adbul Rahman, prime minister of Malaysia, and the members of his party.
It is a source of pride to all of us that in recent years so many parts of the commonwealth have attained national independence and established democratic self government. Now, in this period, they require more than ever time in which to develop viable economies, in which to grapple with their social problems, and, above all, to preserve their territorial integrity and firmly establish parliamentary institutions.
We are glad the prime minister has visited Canada and is meeting with members of our government. I hope that as a result of this visit Canada will be able to play a useful part in helping Malaysia to maintain its independence and develop the way of democratic self government upon which it has set its feet. This party is very glad to welcome the prime minister and our other visitors from Malaysia.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF MALAYSIA AND PARTY
speechtext:
On behalf of our party permit me to say, Mr. Speaker, that it is a distinct honour and privilege to extend our warmest greetings to His Royal Highness Tunku Abdul Rahman, the distinguished prime minister of Malaysia and the members of his party.
We in this country have watched the Tun-ku's statesmanship with deep admiration and respect. All Canadians have felt an anxious concern for the immediate troubles of his country in its struggle for survival against the forces of aggression and neo-imperialism. It is this concern that is so characteristic of a family in which the problems and needs of one can be shared by all. Truly it is this sentiment which is the fibre of this great commonwealth of nations. It is this intangible bond which links men of all races, creeds and colours together, in times of distress as well as in times of peace. I am confident when I say that this link is stronger than ever between the sister countries of Malaysia and Canada.
I join with the Prime Minister and the leaders of other parties in this house in welcoming the prime minister of Malaysia. We know that Malaysia is many thousands of

miles away from us, but all Canadians greet him warmly on his visit to this home away from home. We can only pray that his brief stay in or country will be all he had hoped and, indeed even more.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF MALAYSIA AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are glad to join with our Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in welcoming to Canada the prime minister of Malaysia.
Malaysia and Canada may be far apart if one considers the distance in miles between them, but we are brought closer to one another by the common tie which unites us in the commonwealth of nations.
We are following closely, with sympathy and interest, the struggle put up by the prime minister of Malaysia and his people against international communism.
We pay tribute to the people of Malaysia and their leader, who are in the first line of battle against communism, and we hope our country will be in a position to co-operate with all the nations of the world, and especially the people of Malaysia, in this valiant fight that country is putting up. We are confident that victory will smile on those who fight, and it is the wish that we express to the prime minister and the people of Malaysia.

1964-MID-YEAR REVIEW"
Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): I beg leave to table a report, "Private and Public Investment in Canada- Outlook '64, mid-year review," which summarizes the results of a recent survey undertaken to check on the capital expenditure intentions for the current year.
Does the house give consent?
Agreed.

In view of the significance of this report I should like to make a few brief comments. The report indicates that there has been a remarkable build-up in 1964 capital spending programs since the previous survey was undertaken at the beginning of the year. On the basis of this new informa-

tion on investment plans, total capital outlays anticipated for 1964 amount to $10.8 billion, about $700 million or 7 per cent higher than previously indicated and 16 per cent above actual outlays last year.
This is the greatest year to year increase in capital spending since 1956. Most of the upward adjustment has occurred in the business sector of the economy, where anticipated outlays are now 10 per cent higher than previously estimated and 18 per cent above last year's expenditure. It is particularly noteworthy that capital outlays in manufacturing industries are now expected to approximate $1J billion in 1964, an increase of more than $400 million or 31 per cent from last year's level.
In the case of housing, renewal of the winter incentive program and a stronger trend in starts this spring than was expected earlier has warranted an upward adjustment from 11 per cent to 18 per cent in the estimated increase in work put in place this year compared with last. In the area of institutional and public investment there has been a moderate upward revision in estimated outlays, which are now expected to rise by 9 per cent from a year ago.
The recent acceleration in the pace of capital spending in Canada has far reaching significance for the Canadian economy. For the current year it has given strong impetus to the economy generally and has been an important factor in the relatively sharp-4 per cent-increase in total employment this year compared with last. The 16 per cent increase anticipated in total capital outlays involves a 17 per cent increase in outlays for new machinery and equipment and a 15 per cent increase in expenditure on new construction. The sharp rise in outlays for new machinery and equipment has meant increased activity in equipment producing industries and also helps to account for the sharp growth in imports this year.
Outlays for construction, on the other hand, have a predominantly domestic impact and the substantial increase in this type of expenditure is being reflected in the domestic construction trades and related material producing industries. Some material suppliers, in fact, are encountering difficulty in meeting the added demands. It is possible, therefore, that lengthened delivery dates for items such as structural steel may cause delays on some projects.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should also add an assurance that the upward revision in the total program is not likely to add significantly
Report on Canadian Economic Outlook to the existing demands on resources. Estimates of actual outlays for the early months of 1964 show that capital spending was already running close to the annual rate indicated by the recent survey. Accordingly, realization of this program would involve little further increase beyond the level of activity already under way in the year to date.
The new surge in capital expansion now under way has important implications for future years as well as for the present year. The appearance of so many major new expansion projects throughout Canadian industry can only mean that businessmen look forward with confidence to expanding markets in the years to come. If this judgment is sound it means that conditions of economic slack are giving way to dynamic growth. This new environment brings renewed hope to the growing number of young people coming on to the labour market, and gives promise of a continuing pace of economic advance commensurate with our growing productive capabilities.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the modesty with which he announced the increase in investment, and the Leader of the Opposition for the equal modesty with which he tried to take the credit for it. I should like to say that an increase in capital investment in Canada is, of course, a very good augury, one which we welcome.
There are two factors we must keep in mind. Only by examination of the figures the minister has tabled can we know to what extent these two factors are being realized. The first is whether this increase in capital investment is adequate to provide for full employment and reasonable economic growth. As long as this country has unemployment our economy is not growing fast enough to provide jobs and there is insufficient capital investment. Therefore, while we are pleased that there is an increase in capital investment, we must temper our enthusiasm with the reminder that we have not yet established full employment in Canada nor come close to it.
The second factor, which I think is even more important, is into what channels this


investment is to be directed. Investment by itself without having regard to human welfare and human needs can be a very meaningless thing. We can have a society in which we have adequate filling stations to look after our cars and not enough hospitals to look after our sick, or plenty of supermarkets in which to shop and not enough schools to which to send our children.
If I remember the survey which was made of capital investment for 1964, it was estimated that investment in schools this year would be down substantially. I hope this will not prove to be the case in the figures which the minister has tabled, but if it is the case then it demonstrates that in Canada we need to begin to establish some order of priority in investment so that investment is directed into social capital projects to improve our standard of life and not just our standard of living.

Mr. Speaker, we certainly are pleased with the report by the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicating growing and increasing prosperity in Canada. This can only be for the benefit of all Canadians. However, if the minister would check where the greatest amount of capital development is taking place I am sure he would find that by far the greater part of it, at least on a per capita basis, is in the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta.
We have a long way to go yet in Canada. I would say that when the government is able to announce that the annual increase in the gross national product has reached 10 per cent; when our annual population increase, which involves an expanded immigration policy, is 5 per cent; when 50 per cent of Canadian industry is truly owned by Canadians, and when 200,000 more Canadians now unemployed are put to work, we will really have something to boast about.

Mr. Speaker, we are not too much surprised by the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) concerning investments in Canada, because we think that the increase just announced is but the reflection of a normal development which is due, of course, to the increase in population and to the modernization of means of production.
This is not surprising, because there is nothing surprising in progress; on the contrary, it must be anticipated, for if we do not move forward we can but move back, and then we have a recession.

But what is surprising is to note that the progress announced is only taking place in the material field, that is the investment field. It is the only field where progress is experienced in our economy in general.
As to the other segments of our economy, especially the one affecting more closely the human aspect of our country, it is in regression; according to the latest statistics released on July 22 last, unemployment in Canada had reached an average of 5.2 per cent, or the highest index in our country in the last 22 years.
The number of bankruptcies reported in June in Ontario is probably the largest recorded in that province in many years.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, while the investments are made in our country, the resulting profits leave even faster for other countries, going to foreign capitalists as dividends, interest and profits.
It is true that the investments are made in Canada, but the profits go somewhere else. What good is it then to invest in our country if Canadians do not gain anything by it?
The day the Minister of Trade and Commerce gets up to say that Canadians are responsible for the investments and will get the profits, then he will deserve our congratulations. But as long as it is known that foreigners come to invest in our country and leave with the profits, as long as that situation prevails in Canada there will be no reason to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
We are told that industries are mushrooming and buildings are erected everywhere; however that is not for us but for others, and if the minister wants to be congratulated, he should see to it that investments in Canada are made by and for Canadians. Then we shall be the first to congratulate him. [Text]

Mr. Speaker, I would direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in connection with the Cyprus situation. In view of the statement of Archbishop Makarios in Athens to the effect that Cyprus has not changed its attitude and will refuse to allow Canadian and United Nations troops freedom of movement, is it now the intention of the government to withdraw the Canadian contingent?
I ask that question in view of the obviously inspired story in today's Globe and Mail to the effect that Canadian troops would not be needed in Cyprus after the autumn. Will the minister make a statement and advise us whether this article, which certainly must have come to his attention, is the result of well informed speculation or just pure speculation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN CONTINGENT
speechtext:
I read the article in question. I see no relationship between the article
6060	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry and the headline. I have already indicated that Canada has been in consultation with the other contributors to the force, and that as a member of the United Nations force, whatever the decision is it will be taken by the United Nations and not by any individual country contributing to that force.
With regard to the statement attributed to the head of the government of Cyprus, this statement has not, I am advised by United Nations authorities, been received by them. It was made, as reported in the newspapers, prior to the meeting between the head of the government of Cyprus and the prime minister of Greece. I would be interested in knowing the conclusions reached between the heads of these two governments before I , make any final observation on what might be considered to be the trend of events.
I have already indicated to the house that there are discussions going on elsewhere, and while one would not want to exaggerate the possible consequences of those, I would be distressed if as a result of those discussions there was not progress being made. I want to make it clear that by the terms of section 32 of the agreement as to the status of the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus, which was concluded by an exchange of letters on March 31, 1964, the force and its members together with its service vehicles, vessels, aircraft and equipment shall enjoy freedom of movement throughout Cyprus.
The reported decision, and I emphasize the word "reported", by the government of Cyprus to deny freedom of movement to the United Nations force is clearly contrary to 'the formal agreement entered into with the United Nations. It is contrary also to the spirit and letter of the security council resolution which calls upon the communities in Cyprus, and their leaders, to act with the utmost restraint. The Canadian government has been in communication with the United Nations and is pursuing the matter.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN CONTINGENT
speechtext: How long ago was it since freedom of movement was first denied United Nations forces, particularly the Canadian force?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN CONTINGENT
speechtext: Freedom of access was denied about a week ago. There was an incident previous to that, but generally speaking there has been no position taken against freedom of movement, which is one of the essential terms of the agreement based on the understanding between the secretary general of the United Nations and the government of Cyprus.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN CONTINGENT
speechtext: Does the minister then admit that there has been a change in attitude on the part of Archbishop Makarios, and that today the position of the UN force is that without that freedom of movement it enjoyed to a certain extent in the past, it will not to be able to discharge its responsibilities?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN CONTINGENT
speechtext: I would not agree that the United Nations force, by its very presence, is unable to discharge the responsibility which it has assumed. Undoubtedly the denial of freedom of movement impairs its full opportunity to carry out its mandate. However, I would recall to my right hon. friend that in other peace keeping operations, notably the Congo and even the United Nations emergency force, there were periods of resistance when the force was not able to carry out its responsibilities. If the force in this instance is denied freedom of movement, unfavourable results will not be due to United Nations efforts. I believe that more than ever the United Nations force is required in the circumstances.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN CONTINGENT
speechtext: agree with the minister that the United Nations force is required in Cyprus, but am I to take it from his statement that he does not consider the violation of its solemn obligation by the government of Cyprus to be a serious thing? subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN CONTINGENT
speechtext: Of course I acknowledge it as a serious thing. I said that at the outset in reply to the right hon. gentleman. I simply want to say that bringing the various offices of the Department of National Health and Welfare, previously distributed
fMr. Maclnnis.]
across Ottawa, under one roof is a very sensible move. When I first became minister of the department I undertook to try to visit all branches of the department situated in various spots in Ottawa with a view to meeting the personnel and seeing the quarters in which they were working, and I found that many of those quarters were of a deplorable character. They were not proper office accommodations at all and, as I say, I think it is a sensible move to put them under one roof. I recall that people came to meetings from all over Ottawa and took some time to get there. There was a considerable waste of time on the part of senior officials in this way, and I think this new move will bring about much more efficient operation of the department.
It certainly strikes me, in view of the description in last evening's Citizen, of the minister's personal office, that she will probably have the most plush executive suite in Ottawa. Possibly these new quarters will provide the tranquil atmosphere which will help the minister to clear her thinking on so many problems, because I do not think clear thinking has been overly evident in the past. I can just picture the minister sauntering around the observation promenade looking over the Gatineau hills deep in thought and coming up with yet another pension plan. Each plan was supposed to be the ultimate in pension schemes, and I am wondering when we are going to get the final one. The white paper which has been promised for months now should surely be in our hands, and I am trusting that the minister will intimate when it will be. The Prime Minister indicated last week, I think, that we would have this white paper very shortly, and I am hoping the minister will indicate the exact date so we will know where we are going.
The government has steadfastly refused to bring forward its regular spending program, and I am wondering whether the government is hoping to cram these estimates, involving billions of dollars, down our throats in the last few days of the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Following your example.
"Pass them or else".

I believe that only nine days have been spent on main estimates so far this session, and we have been meeting since February 18. We have had three supply motions, and 15 departments have been called in those motions. Two departments have been completed, agriculture and post office. Ex-

temal affairs has been transferred to the standing committee on external affairs after a one day debate in the committee of the whole house. Public works has been before the house for one day, as has northern affairs, on last Friday. Ten other departments have been available, yet we have only had nine days of study of the government's main estimates.
Mr. Chairman, some research has been done in previous years in this regard, and I have before me the figures for other non-election years; 1955, 1956, 1959, 1960 and the session 1960-61. I have a record of the number of sitting days, the total number of days spent on main estimates and the percentage of the session occupied with main estimates. By the 115th sitting day, which in this session will be tomorrow, the number of days spent on main estimates in 1955 was 17, and five departments had been sent to standing or special committees. In 1956, 20 days at this same period had been spent on main estimates, and five departments had gone to standing or special committees. In 1959 we had spent 27 days on main estimates and six departments had been referred to standing or special committees. In 1960 some 25 days had been spent on main estimates, and five departments had gone to standing or special committees. In the session 1960-61 some 28 days had been spent on main estimates, and two departments had gone to standing or special committees. In this session, by tomorrow, the 115th day, nine days, as I have said, have been spent on main estimates; and one department, the Department of External Affairs, has gone to the standing committee. Usually about one third to one half of the time at this stage of the session has been allotted to consideration of main estimates. The last supply motion we had was on May 26; these estimates have all been before us since.
I think I should stress what is the main function of government. We really would not have to meet if it were not to pass main estimates, to pass the order of supply and put the spending program of the government before the houses of parliament for study and examination. Therefore why have we not been given the opportunity of discussing these main estimates? To me there can be only one of two reasons, Mr. Chairman; either the government hope to get most of them through in the last few days of the session, or they expect to call an election before the completion of the session. The reason has to be one of those two, as I see it.
I do not see how we can excuse the government for not having brought its spending
Interim Supply
program before parliament. It is fine to bring on legislation; that is a necessary function of government. But the real reason parliament meets is to study the spending of the government for the ensuing year. In my opinion the government has been very negligent in this respect. Mr. Chairman, because Waterloo North is one of the best and most diversified farming areas in Canada, I have been particularly interested in reading the parliamentary committee's second report on pesticides. In Waterloo North we have a high degree of industralization with secondary industry, including one of Canada's largest manufacturers of basic herbicides and other pesticide chemicals. This operation is located in my home town of Elmira, Ontario, and is a $3 million plant.

The committee's studies have served to focus attention on several important considerations relative to the continuing wide scale use of pesticides. I am encouraged to find that the committee feels generally that the danger to human health from the present use of pesticides is small if they are used as directed. The legislation in Canada, both generally and in relation to its enforcement, appears to have protected the people of Canada to date from major hazards from pesticides. These two statements by the committee are most significant when it is realized the part pesticides play in agricultural production and natural resources as well as human health and comfort today.
A compilation of estimated losses caused by insects, plant diseases, weeds and rodents in Canada in 1955 placed the total damage, including the cost of control measures, at $1.25 billion annually. This is a terrific amount. Losses due to weeds exceed $1,000 yearly for the average farm. Yield reduction due to weeds in cereals in Manitoba is an estimated 14 per cent. Returns from herbicide treatment in 1963 have been conservatively set at $32 million, with an investment of only $6 million in herbicides. The benefits from pesticides used in agriculture have been so apparent to users that few detailed statistical studies have been needed to demonstrate the dollar values derived.
There are no cases on record of human fatalities resulting from the proper use of agricultural chemicals. Human error remains the most frustrating factor to be overcome in making chemicals thoroughly safe to manufacture, distribute and use. Public enlightenment, sensible legislation and government vigilance play vital roles in safeguarding the public health. An additional force for safety is the industry's regard for its own good name. I note in the report that the committee found that, generally speaking, government and industry are well aware of the potential dangers from pesticides, but the public does need education in these fields. More should be done in this regard. Directions and precautions on containers are of little use if they are not read by the purchaser.
The recommendations to the federal government for the formation of a committee on pesticides with representatives from agriculture, national health and welfare, fisheries, forestry, northern affairs and national research council should be acted upon. The recommendation that the pest control act be amended to prevent the importation of pesticides not registered under the act from a country outside of Canada would seem neces-

sary. I should hope this would not prevent importations for purposes of experimental research by government or industrial agencies.
Two recommendations made by the committee to the senior government are, I think most important. Enforcement of federal regulations should be strict and followed by prosecutions where warranted. The other recommendation was that the committee on pesticides should study the requirements for staff, equipment and facilities of the federal government departments in relation to their duties connected with pesticides. I am pleased to note that the Department of National Health and Welfare has already taken positive steps toward improving their staff and facilities in order to meet this need.
The committee's suggestion that consideration be given to the licensing of commercial sprayers of pesticides, based on proper training and expert supervision, would seem to be a desirable direction in which to work. The committee has recognized that this subject is under both federal and provincial jurisdiction, and recommends the study of mutual interest areas in an effort to improve the present relationships, with the aim of providing consumer safety in foods and cooperation and respect of the producer.
As the means of food production become increasingly complex, interdependent and effective, the possibility of overlapping and contradictory legislation between levels of government arises, with the confusion and inefficiency such a situation inevitably brings with it. It becomes increasingly Important, therefore, that mutual interest areas be dealt with in a spirit of full co-operation and consideration.
The committee has noted the need for setting standards and procedures for poison control centres. I do not think this can be too strongly emphasized. I believe that at the present time we have one such centre at the Toronto Sick Children's hospital. I have mentioned only a few of the matters that I believe to be significant in the committee's report, and this house is indebted to the members of the committee for the work they have done.

It is an honour and a privilege to make what is traditionally known in this place as a maiden speech. I would like to speak on a subject which is, I believe, both important and timely.
One of the great problems facing the Canadian people and the Canadian government today is the problem of the mentally ill, the people whose resources are lost to themselves and to the country. I am not going to delve far back into the dark regions of the past to describe the snake pit existence to which these people were often condemned; suffice it to say that in this field there has been more ignorance, more neglect, and more outright rejection of the sick person than in any other field of human illness.
In the first part of this century there was an advance made in the understanding of the nature and incidence of mental illness. The casualty experiences of personnel during world war I revealed in a convincing manner that everyone has a breaking point in response to stress. This realization was the birth of our modern scientific physiological approach; the beginning of a new era for those whose human resources lay paralysed in the grip of their anxieties.
But it was only a beginning, for progress was slow. Both medical and lay-people were concerned with the separation of the sane from the insane, with the segregation of those who deviated in a disturbing manner from socially accepted types of behaviour. This was rationalized on the grounds of protection for the so-called normal element of society. People generally were unenlightened, afraid of what they saw. They felt relieved when a disturbed relative or friend was put away in a mental hospital.
Overcrowding in mental hospitals was increased by the addition of emotionally crippled veterans, those who were suffering from wounds of the mind and the spirit. There was inadequate staff to provide for their treatment and care.
In post-war years, individuals came forward who made history in their contribution to the organization and development of psychiatric care in Canada. One of these, Dr. Clarence Hincks, conducted surveys of mental hospitals and made recommendations to provincial governments. In 1918 he organ-

ized the national committee of mental hygiene, which was eventually succeeded by the Canadian mental health association.
In Saskatchewan, Dr. MacNeill pioneered in the field of mental health, and the MacNeill clinic in Saskatoon is a tribute to his early work in the province.
From segregation of patients there began to be a discernible shift in emphasis to more humane care. New methods of treatment were introduced. New mental hospitals were built, treatment clinics were established, and medical schools set up departments of psychiatry. By 1939, general hospitals were beginning to develop psychiatric services. The private practice of psychiatry was by now established and recognized as a legitimate specialty.
Another world war on a much wider and more devastating scale demonstrated even more forcibly the vulnerability of the individual to stress. There was a concentration of overseas psychiatric medical teams to meet this emergency in the armed forces. In the process of this experience, there developed a more penetrating breakthrough in the understanding of emotional disturbances, and consequently a better approach to those who were afflicted. There was also some effort made in the prevention of mental illness by attempts to place personnel suitably. This advancing enlightenment began to sift through the general population of the country.
In the post-war years the Canadian mental health association, a voluntary organization, was establishing provincial divisions and local branches. Their activity did much to promote public interest and understanding in the field of mental health, and resulted in a program of information and services which furthered public education and directly assisted in the care and comfort of the sick in mental hospitals. Impetus was given to research by the setting up of the national mental health research fund. The Canadian association for retarded children is another voluntary organization which was organized in Canada after world war II by a group of parents and friends of mentally retarded children. It has divisions in most provinces. It has established and operated excellent programs for the mentally retarded, including classes for those excluded from regular schools-like the John Dolan school in Saskatoon-recreation centres, day care programs and sheltered workshops. Pressure from this association has done much to inspire governments to contribute more to the education and training of retarded children, and counselling services for their parents.

There has been an increasing co-operation between government health authorities, professional groups, the Canadian Mental Health Association, the Canadian Association for Retarded Children and other organizations. Lay groups have shown a developing interest and concern in the mental health field, and are increasingly demonstrating a desire to participate in programs at a community level. We seem to be in a time of change when people are attempting to break down old barriers and are seeking new ways of involvement in social programs.
What is the situation in Canada today for the mentally ill? What are some of the significant trends we can observe in modern day psychiatry, and what are the problems that must be met? There are approximately 75,000 patients in mental institutions in Canada today, or 3.7 beds per thousand population, at a cost of less than $5 per bed per day. In general hospitals there are some 90,000 patients receiving treatment for physical ailments, or 5.5 beds per thousand population at a cost of over $20 per bed per day. The present total cost of general hospital beds in Canada comes to over $800 million a year, whereas the total cost of beds for mental patients runs at approximately $130 million. It must be said that there is a greater increase in cost of operation for general hospitals. Over a five year period operating costs of hospitals have increased around 85 per cent but the operating costs of mental hospitals have increased by less than 25 per cent. Also about
10,000	mental patients are admitted to hospitals acutely ill, and most of the beds in general hospitals are acute beds, which are more expensive; but over and above this there is a wide discrepancy in the quality of the facilities and care provided for the two groups of patients. All provinces spend more than three times as much per day for each general hospital as they do for mental hospitals. Yet it has been conclusively demonstrated that improved facilities, attractive surroundings and competent professional care make for more effective treatment. They are an important part of the psychiatric treatment program.
Our mentally sick people should not be treated as second class citizens. Why should they be segregated to lower class institutions? Mr. Chairman, this whole question of treatment of the mentally ill is primarily a segregation problem, and it is a segregation problem that can involve anyone-because mental illness knows no colour, class or creed. It can come to any one of us, and when it

does the gate closes and segregation becomes a cruel fact. People who suffer from acute mental and physical diseases are all very sick people and should be treated in the same hospitals. The distinction now made between the two types of illness is a false one and discriminates unfairly against those suffering from acute mental disorders.
There are at the present time only 2,000 beds set aside in over 50 of our Canadian general hospitals for the treatment of mentally disturbed people. More than 15,000 people are admitted to these wards annually. This represents more than half the number admitted per year to all mental hospitals in Canada. There is a faster turnover. Patients admitted to these wards are generally treated by physicians who are specializing in psychiatry, but in some instances the directors of these units do invite general practitioners to admit and treat their own patients under supervision. This has worked out well in the University Hospital at Saskatoon, where Dr. D. G. McKerracher is professor and head of the department of psychiatry at the University of Saskatchewan. He has given warm encouragement to general practitioners to gain in-service training in psychiatry by participation in this program. But aside from the 2,000 psychiatry beds in a general hospital set-up, there are not adequate facilities now for the treatment of people with acute mental disorders. We need to provide in a general hospital enough beds to treat these people. Here is a chance for government to face up to the reality of what is needed for the acutely ill psychiatric patient. First priority should go to the treatment of the very sick, and they should not be segregated from other patients. There should be at least .5 beds per thousand population, or 10,000 beds in general hospitals as a minimum in Canada for these patients. This figure could well run to 12,000.
What are the advantages of the treatment of acute mental disorders in a general hospital? There is a closer relationship of the psychiatrist with other medical people, with other doctors in the hospital. There is better integration of psychiatry and general medicine, more ready acceptance of psychiatric treatment by people outside the hospital who are learning to regard it as another form of medical treatment, and a faster return of the patient to the community. On this kind of ward there is a closer relationship with general practitioners and with other community personnel such as clergy, teachers, local pub-

lie health people, V.O.N. nurses, etc., including family and friends who may well benefit from their visits to the ward and develop a much better approach to the patient.
The Canadian psychiatric association has recommended that all hospitals of more than 200 beds should develop psychiatric wards as soon as possible. Others feel that any hospital over 100 beds should have a psychiatric unit. The Hall commission report advocates this figure. When we have dealt with the hospital wards for the acute patients and provided them with 10,000 to 12,000 general hospital beds, this leaves around 65,000 patients in Canadian mental institutions. This is a most important problem, which requires special consideration and which I do not propose to develop here. We are then left with some 50,000 patients in Canadian mental institutions. These are the chronically ill and the aged. Of these, 10,000 to 12,000-that is .6 per thousand population-are so sick they cannot be cared for except by good nurses and good doctors in attendance. And these people are in mental hospitals. They are the old people with poor circulatory systems, who have confused minds and broken down old brains. They cannot be at home; they cannot stay in boarding homes or nursing homes. These people belong in the chronic care wings of general hospitals, just as much as patients who have chronic heart and arthritic conditions. They need constant professional care with internists and psychiatrists available for ready consultation.
The rest of the aged and those who are chronically ill should be in the community, not in mental hospitals. Partly as a result of a lower death rate, there is an increase in the number of old people now in mental hospitals. Old people with no place to go could be in a home for the aged. do follow-up work; first, to help rehabilitate acute patients after their discharge from hospital, and second to help keep the chronically ill and the aged out of hospital and in the community. The Hall commission report makes strong recommendations in this regard.
If in Canada we were recruiting an adequate number of people to train for this war on the poverty of our human resources, we could use postgraduate students in psychiatry and the social sciences to assist in the care of these people and at the same time relate this experience to research projects. This would enable us to learn much more about the potentialities of the aged and the chronically ill. But at the present time there are not enough residents and postgraduate students, and there is not the set-up in the community to absorb and train these people. If the government could do something to increase the prestige of personnel trained in the care of the mentally ill, more would enter this field. We need a declaration of interest by government in this group of mental health personnel-psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses and social workers. The government should give leadership in pointing up the need for such trained people at the community level. But there have to be incentives for training.
More psychiatrists are needed. There are only 600 qualified psychiatrists in Canada, about one for every 30,000 population. Only about half of these are conducting a private practice. The remainder are in government service and receive a lower income than their colleagues. Psychiatrists cannot look after all the mentally ill people, or even a reasonable number of them. Nor will they ever be able to do so. They cannot at present even provide adequate consultation services for general practitioners and other specialists, let alone provide individual care on a cradle to the grave basis.
It seems logical that most psychiatrists should function largely in a consultative capacity. The number of qualified psychiatrists in Canada needs to be doubled, and those who work for government should receive salaries that compare with the incomes of their medical colleagues. They should be available to help social agencies, law enforcement agencies, and other people who are dealing with the confused, the anxious and the depressed. This contact also gives an opportunity for teaching which is very much needed.
General practitioners in Canada see thousands and thousands of people suffering from mental disorders, and they will continue to see thousands and thousands of these people.

And they should be encouraged to do so. They are treating at present over 90 per cent of the people with psychiatric complaints. In most cases they are not prepared, not helped, and not adequately paid for it. They do not receive recognition for the great service they perform. The general practitioner sees an average of five of these patients per day. Since there are some 15,000 practising doctors in Canada, this means that 75,000 patients with psychiatric problems are seen each day in doctors' offices across the country. Both medical students and general practitioners need more psychiatric training than they now receive. More than half of those graduating from medical schools will be family doctors, and will be inadequately prepared to give psychiatric treatment; and yet they are the ones who will take on by far the greatest load of out-patient psychiatric care. The family doctor knows the patient's family. He knows the social and economic background, and he enjoys the patient's confidence. He does a good job, but he needs help. He should be able to get psychiatric consultation when he needs it, and the social services of the community should be readily available to help him with his patient problems.
Almost every mentally sick person who has had hospital treatment needs some form of rehabilitation, some kind of help in his effort to fit once more into the community. But he does not get the kind of consideration a physically handicapped patient receives. Once more he is segregated, stigmatized, and too little interest is taken by all concerned in his chances for future training and employment. He is in fact often rejected.
Britain is far ahead of us in this field of rehabilitation of the mentally ill. There, many mental hospitals have made arrangements with commercial firms who employ former patients in large numbers. A few patients are admitted to sheltered workshops but only on a temporary basis. There are no sheltered workshops in Canada that provide permanent employment to people with chronic mental handicaps, people who may never work on a competitive basis. These people are now on municipal relief and lead a life of idleness, discouragement and deterioration. Their potentialities are wasted, not only to themselves but to the community.
Mentally handicapped people need encouragement and incentives to work, and per-

manent sheltered employment set up either by state or private organizations could provide an answer to their dilemma. Those who remain at a low level of work performance could continue to receive some municipal social assistance, but undoubtedly some would benefit from the therapeutic effect of paid work geared to their ability to perform, and might very well become increasingly productive. The Glenside hospital in Bristol has an active industrial program which began in 1958, and was initiated by Dr. Donald Early, a consultant psychiatrist. By 1962 there were 500 chronically ill and hopeless patients involved in it. Of these 500 working patients, 400 became paid workers inside the hospital for commercial firms, and 100 patients were working for pay outside the hospital. A company in Bristol called the industrial therapy organization opened up business in a former schoolhouse and also operated a nearby car wash. The 100 patients began to work here, some of them sleeping at the hospital and some sleeping out, but all working a 40-hour week. The Bristol council made plans to build hostels for those who were able to live outside the hospital.
After a four year period of this industrial therapy program, 136 of these chroncially ill and hopeless patients were discharged from the hospital and were on their own, most of them employed full time. Dr. Early considers this kind of therapy more beneficial than pills. Only the very old who are physically ill and are unable to work do not take part in the programs. There is much that can be learned if governments will sponsor the adoption of new and experimental programs in an effort to investigate and reclaim the most valuable of all our resources, the resources that are within people.

Mr. Chairman, I must congratulate the hon. member for Saskatoon immediately on one of the most thoughtful speeches that have been heard in the house in a long time. I want to assure her that to the ragged and tattered fighters of the second session of the twenty sixth parliament a speech like this comes at a good time, not only in terms of giving us a breath of fresh air but as an example that we perhaps might emulate when we are not scrapping.
It is in this happy mood that I want to discuss for a few moments some of the things that have happened in the Department of National Health and Welfare. I do so at this time because, as the minister well knows, this is the first opportunity that any member has had to take a look at the spending in this department. Either because the minister is unwilling or unable to convince her colleagues, her main estimates have not been presented to the house for discussion, and I want to take this opportunity to say a few things that cannot be said at any other time.
I know that already the press has started to accuse the opposition of conducting a filibuster merely because we do not automatically grant to the federal government over $700 million in spending authority. In today's Ottawa Citizen there is a headline, "Tory Filibuster Starts", obviously written by the Prime Minister's nephew. I for one am quite prepared to take some time to have a look at how this $700 million is going to be used by the government. I am not ashamed to hold up this matter for a while in order to say a few things that are of importance not only to the people of my constituency but to all the people of Canada. Surely the hon. lady must be relieved when she looks back and thinks what might have happened if the house had gone right ahead with the first Canada pension plan legislation and had approved that first wretched and fumbling attempt by the government to provide some sort of intelligent social security measure. I do not want to say any more about that because I do not want to irritate the hon. lady. In fact, I want to congratulate her, and I do so seriously because she is the first minister to allow the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to participate in federal-provincial

conferences by means of direct representation. This may seem a minor point to many people but in fact it is a tremendous step forward. The hon. member for Yukon and I have asked the government some 30 times in the twenty sixth parliament to permit this. The hon. lady made an announcement to that effect the other day and I want to tell her sincerely that by that one act she has certainly endeared herself to me.
The hon. lady and I have had our little disagreements in the past and we undoubtedly will have more in the future. In fact, we may have more later this afternoon. But I want her to know that I am a big enough man to embrace her principles and her ideas wholeheartedly with regard to the matter of allowing the people of the north to be represented at federal-provincial conferences. I do not think the hon. member for Yukon and I will really take the next step, but I suppose we could insist that in future all such conferences be called federal-provincial-territorial conferences. I do not think we will do that.
The other day the hon. member for Port Arthur said that members of parliament when they get up to speak never suggest ways of saving money to the government, but instead ask for more and more for their own constituencies. While I have been guilty of this in the past, today I want to suggest to the minister one place where she can save $84 million of the taxpayers' money. I am going to tell her how and I want her to do this. I want her to scrap the building of the new Charles Camsell hospital in Edmonton, Alberta, which will cost the taxpayers some $84 million. I should like to give the history of this matter and I can do so very quickly.
The Charles Camsell hospital was never a hospital in the first place. It was built for other purposes and it was gradually expanded and extended, much in the way that a shack sometimes becomes a house in the more northerly parts of Canada merely by additions being made to it. This hospital has been used to treat Eskimo and Indian people. They are flown from northern Alberta and from the Yukon and Northwest Territories to the hospital in Edmonton for treatment.
The officials in the minister's department wanted a new building, and they wanted a new one for good reason. The existing Charles Camsell building is old and it is a firetrap, as I mentioned earlier. The hon. member for Athabasca happens to know it well. This building was never intended for a hospital in the first place. It is a disgrace that the
Interim Supply
government of Canada should be treating people in a building such as this.
However this does not mean you have to build a new one. As so often happens in government, when something is not good enough the departmental officials do not say, "Well, do we need it at all?" They say, "Let us build a bigger and better one." At any rate, the Glassco commission took a very careful look at this building and the need for it. They came up with some recommendations to which I should like to refer. They recommend that the minister or the government do not proceed with the building of this hospital. They say it is unnecessary and would preserve the kind of racial segregation of which no Canadian citizen can be proud.
The Glassco commission recommendations certainly were received by the previous administration. I know from talks I had at that time with the then minister of national health and welfare, and since then, that the administration of that day decided they would not go ahead with this plan but would review it very carefully before spending this amount of money. The Glassco commission found, first of all, that there were sufficient empty t.b. beds in the province of Alberta to accommodate any Indian or Eskimo people that might be admitted in the forthcoming year. This is very significant because, as hon. members may know, the treatment of Indian and Eskimo peoples has been done in hospitals separated from the rest of the treatment hospitals in the province, ostensibly because the Eskimo and Indian people are shy; that they prefer to be in hospitals with other Eskimo and Indian people. Well, this has never been my experience, Mr. Chairman, during my years of work with the Eskimo and Indian people. It may have been a valid statement at some point. Suffice to say it certainly is not valid any longer.
Even if it were valid, even if they were shy or reluctant to go into hospitals with whites-if we can use that word, and I do not like it-then surely the solution to the problem is to change the milieu in which they would find themselves, change the attitude of the white administrators and set things up in the hospital so the people who come in there who happen to have other than white skin and these funny round eyes are not made to feel uncomfortable. This would be better than spending $8.5 million. The Glassco commission suggested that the department should get out of this kind of hospital immediately. On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member does not wish to mislead the committee and people outside this chamber who will read Hansard. He has done something here that I should explain for the benefit of people who will read Hansard, so that they will know what he is up to. He has tried to create the impression that he was giving the Minister of National Health and Welfare an opportunity to answer a rhetorical question he put when, by his own act, he chose to prevent her from answering the question he was putting on the record. I do not intend to take a lecture from the hon. gentleman raised on a phony point of order. I am prepared to defend my conduct against him or anyone else, and may I say I hope members on the treasury benches, when they get up to speak, will take advantage of the opportunity and say something. Yesterday we asked the Minister of Labour what he was doing about the mollycoddling of Hal Banks. But did we get any information? No. He replied, but he told us nothing. I say this to the President of the Privy Council: Don't use these phony

points of order to lecture a young fellow like me who is trying to make a case on behalf of his people. The hon. gentleman spoke about reading Hansard. Well, if he will read Hansard he will find I have made a very logical case, pointing out how this government can save $8J million. I want to know whether this decision was taken because of pressure brought to bear by the people who operate this sanatorium, which has 250 empty beds but will admit white people only. Is this why we now have to build a new hospital to treat Eskimos and Indians? Or did the Liberal government in Alberta come to the minister and say: It would be a great thing for all of us if that $8J million could be spent here in advance of another election which is coming up; it would show Alberta that even though we do not have too many seats out here, we have not been forgotten. Is this why it was done? I ask these questions because the decision was taken in the face of recommendations which were nonpartisan in nature, knowing it could only damage prospects of the people who live in my part of the country.

Would the hon. member permit a question? He indicated that this is a recommendation of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I wonder whether he is suggesting that this recommendation was a partisan one.

I would never accuse the hon. lady of partisanship. No. The matter had been under review by the previous administration, and the thing was cancelled. The Glassco commission had recommended that it be cancelled. Then, lo and behold, after a visit by the hon. lady, the announcement was made that the hospital was going to be built. The hon. member for York-Scarborough can draw any conclusion he likes as to what went on.
There is another question I want to ask. Do we have to build this hospital because the medical officers and others who now work in the Camsell hospital do not want to move north, though if they were to move to the end of the steel it would mean the saving of many thousands of dollars in transportation costs alone? Are these people afraid to go north? Who is insisting that this hospital be built in Edmonton? I want to suggest that whatever reasons there may have been for this kind of conduct in the past, they are no longer valid. If we spend this $8i million in the way proposed, right after our Prime Minister has been lecturing Southern Rhodesia on how to handle race problems, we

shall have a black mark against his twenty sixth parliament which will go a lot deeper than any kind of inability to do work. There is no justification for this decision, no matter how you look at it, whether from the point of view of race or colour or from the point of view of economics, and I am amazed that the President of the Privy Council should have leaped to his feet in the way he did- he, the wielder of the great axe against spending-in order to defend the minister on a question of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to digress a bit from such an interesting subject as national health and welfare, but I do feel that, after what the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) said yesterday in this house, while making charges concerning the way our government treated Mr. Banks, I would be remiss, in my capacity as Minister of Justice, if I did not rise, not only to refute those charges, but also to indicate quite clearly just how much the comments made by the hon. member for Bow River are unfounded.
I regret to speak today in his absence, but I have an excuse for so doing inasmuch as he himself chose to make those remarks about the actions of the Department of Justice while I was detained in my office. It so happened then that, when he spoke, I was not present. Therefore, although he is not here today, I am duty bound to give the house the full particulars it was then entitled to have.
The hon. member, and up to a certain point also the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), charged the government with having, when proceedings were taken against Mr. Hal Banks, pampered him -for that is the word he used, "pampered"- with having treated him in a special way which, it was even sometimes implied, was against the law.
Mr. Chairman, when the present government had to carry out its duty following the tabling of the Norris report, it assumed its full responsibilities under the circumstances, and to the best of its knowledge and, above all, in keeping with the opportunities afforded by those circumstances, it discharged those responsibilities to the best of its ability.
Interim Supply
When we came into power, we inherited a situation already existing long before 1962, when the Norris commission was established, a situation which the previous administration knew very well, since as early as 1958 and 1959, it was aware of the activities of Banks and of the problems they could entail. But all the same, the previous government allowed this situation to prevail and to deteriorate to such an extent that during 1962, the conditions on the St. Lawrence seaway and the great lakes became unbearable and that even an actual congestion of maritime traffic had to be corrected.
About Mr. Banks and the attitude of the then government, I must point out that being in possession, of course, as early as 1958, of information that should have been looked into more fully, the government did not see fit at the time to conduct an investigation which would have made it easier to bring Banks before the court than in 1963 and 1964, since those events had just occurred. It would have been easier to check the facts and to have the proper witnesses appear instead of having to overcome very serious difficulties, as we had to do, because we managed to perform the seemingly impossible task of bringing Banks before the court five or six years after the offences were committed, for which it had not been deemed advisable to prosecute him.
If we consider what happened in 1962-and I only mention it because of the accusation of delay in carrying out a warrant obtained by my predecessor Mr. Lionel Chevrier, following the Norris report-it is noted that if at that time, Banks had been prosecuted, the circumstances would have been much different from those we had to face.
Finally, in the summer of 1962, an intolerable situation existed on the great lakes; in 1963, as soon as the Norris report was published, as soon as the government could do something, legal action was taken and complaints were lodged after the government had retained the best Toronto and Montreal lawyers. So, this government is the first to do something about Mr. Banks; this government is the first to assume its responsibilities and prosecute Mr. Banks with the results we know: decisions were taken.
I cannot go beyond that, because an appeal has now been lodged. But I thought I ought to mention that fact because of the accusation which has been made. If proceedings have been delayed at a given moment, and this was admitted at the time, it was to allow the

Interim Supply
trustees to start their "operations" and restore peace on the seaway.
I thought I ought to mention that accusation and it is the only reason why, as I said, I did so here, for I do not want to discuss fully a matter which is sub judice. The only reason why I intervened is because of the accusation made that, after having instituted legal proceedings, we had played into the hands of Mr. Banks by delaying somewhat the serving of the warrant of arrest which brought him before the court.
Constant attempts were made, through the hon. member for Bow River to create the impression that we had acted in such a way as to treat Mr. Banks as a spoiled child and, I repeat, as to cajole him. It was said for instance that at the time of his appeal against the sentence passed on him, Mr. Banks enjoyed discrimination because the government did not see fit to include in the bond a provision to prevent him from leaving the territorial limits of Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think it is essential to note that the crown, on the occasion of the appeal made by Banks and of the request for bail he made before the chief justice of the court of appeal of the province of Quebec, the crown objected that no bail should be granted in the case of Mr. Hal Banks.
I must quote, to have them put on the record, excerpts from the sentence passed on May 8, 1964, by the hon. chief justice of the court of appeal, Mr. Justice Lucien Tremblay whom, I am quite proud to proclaim loudly in this house, is one of the most experienced jurists within our superior courts, one of those who practice their profession with the utmost objectivity and the utmost understanding.
In the first paragraph of the sentence, here is what could be found:
The crown is opposed to any bail. In addition, it holds that, should I feel I have to grant the request, I should ask for a bond of $50,000.
I will stop a moment and ask those who accuse the government of having pampered Mr. Banks when proceedings were instituted against him, this question: Is asking the court to refuse someone bail equivalent to granting him preferential treatment? Is it granting him preferential treatment to say: If, in the administration of justice, the president of the court of appeal feels that bail can be granted, that bail should be set at $50,000 or more?
I say it is quite the opposite of what the hon. member of Bow River is accusing us of doing.

Further on, the judge gives the reasons why, in his opinion, he is justified first in granting bail and second in setting it at $25,000; he sets that amount at $25,000 and
says:
If I refuse to set him free temporarily and his appeal is granted, he will have suffered a few months' imprisonment that would be hard to justify. If I grant his request and his appeal is rejected, the only result will be to postpone by a few months the beginning of his sentence (section 624, Criminal Code).
And later he says this:
It is important however to set bail high enough to make as sure as it is humanly possible that he will not try to evade justice. I feel that an amount of $25,000 will do it.
The chief justice of the appeal court then summarized the whole case. He stressed the purpose of the bail: to ensure that the person against whom there is an appeal will be sufficiently interested by the said bail to come forward for the hearing of the appeal, failing which his $25,000 will be forfeited or confiscated.
In my opinion, this is sufficient guarantee that Mr. Banks will be in court when the appeal is heard on September 14, 1964. Mr. Banks will surrender to justice at that time.
According to some people, the crown failed to use the proper bail form which would have precluded Mr. Banks from leaving the country. The house should know that the crown used the proper form, the one which is prescribed in the Criminal Code of Canada. Mr. Chairman, please refer to form 28 which, according to the circumstances, may be used in the case of a person who has been com-mited for trial or where the accused has appealed the sentence. It will be noted that paragraph (g) provides exactly how form 28 should be used in appeal cases.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Wool-liams) referred to the form which provides that "the accused may not leave the country without leave of permission." According to him, this meant that Mr. Banks was prevented from leaving the territorial jurisdiction of Canada.
If we take form (c), which applies only in cases where the accused is not on appeal but sent back to his trial, we see that even in this case, there is no prohibition in the code, to the effect of preventing the accused from leaving, when under bail, the territorial jurisdiction of Canada.
I quote from the form used to that effect:
Now, therefore, the condition of the above written recognizance is that (if the accused appears at that court, or if, having re-elected under part XVI, he appears before the presiding

judge at the time and place fixed for his trial) and takes his trial on the indictment that is found against him and does not depart the said court without leave, the said recognizance is void;-
It is clear that the purpose of this bail is that the accused undertakes to be present when his trial will be called and that as long as the trial will last, he will not get away from the court.
This does not mean that until his trial is called, he is denied the right to leave the country. I merely mean that if we look at the bail form prescribed in the case of a person who is under trial or the form prescribed in the case where a person appeals against a decision which finds him guilty, there is no provision restricting the right of the accused, the appellant, of staying in the country or leaving it.
I have here a true copy of the recognizance bond which contains the judgment to which I referred you a while ago, and we see that it is clear.
I mentioned the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition to the effect that the provision restricting the right of circulating freely inside as well as outside the territorial limits of Canada would have been taken out of the recognizance bond. Now, we see in the recognizance bond that no provision was eliminated in the text and that it is exactly the same as prescribed by the Criminal Code.
It is important today for the house to know that as far as the recognizance bond is concerned, all the government can be accused of concerning Mr. Banks is that the provisions of the law were respected, and as Minister of Justice I am always delighted and happy when I am accused of respecting the provisions of the law.
Finally, there is the confusion spread by the speech of the hon. member for Bow River -and I regret that the Leader of the Opposition did not point it out-that is, the relation which would exist between the proceedings instituted against Banks before the appeal court and the proceedings under which a warrant has now been issued by the superior court of the province of Quebec.
I must say that the federal government has nothing to do with the proceedings mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River which resulted in the issuance of the warrant under which Banks is now sought out. It is a purely civil procedure taken against Banks by a company named Upper Lakes Shipping Company, because it claimed that Banks neglected or refused to submit to an injunction of the 20220-385J
Interim Supply
superior court of the province of Quebec. As a result of a request made by this company, and by virtue of clause 957 and the following clause, especially clause 971 of the code of civil procedure, which is surely not part of the Criminal Code and does not come under federal jurisdiction, as was claimed last week, the warrant was issued by the superior court and handed over to the sheriff. Clause 971 reads as follows:
Any person against whom an injunction is directed who infringes or refuses to obey it, or any person who, although not named or described therein, knowingly contravenes its commands, is subject to a fine not exceeding two thousand dollars, payable to the crown, with or without imprisonment for a period not exceeding sixty days, without prejudice to the right of the party aggrieved to recover damages.
It is obvious that this is a purely civil procedure, on which may be grafted, if so desired, an action for damages initiated by the claimant against the person thus prosecuted.
Under the circumstances, I thought it was my responsibility to establish the required distinction, and to prove that by not attempting to intervene in the execution of the warrant obtained by a strictly civil party, in a strictly civil case, between the Upper Lakes Shipping Company and Hal Banks, the federal government was not remiss in its duty. Quite the contrary, if it had done so, it would have been guilty of interference in the field of civil cases and the administration of justice between civil parties in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to labour the point, but I think that if we all look objectively at the facts and try to analyse them in the light of justice and with a critical sense prompted by justice, we must come to only one conclusion, that is not only did the government not cajole Banks, but it took all the required recourses and steps in accordance with the prescribed procedure within its jurisdiction.
In addition, I must inform the house that, if necessary, this government will continue to act in the same way concerning Banks or anyone else who must be prosecuted.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. minister allow me a question?

Mr. Chairman, can the hon. minister tell the house why the federal government assumed the responsibility for lodging complaints against Banks instead of leaving the whole matter, that is lodging
