speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the answer to this question is very simple.
The situation concerned the government and was under its jurisdiction because being connected with the safety of navigation in Canada it was a matter of waterways and water transport.
Moreover, following the tabling of the Norris report, which had been prepared by a commission set up by the former Conservative government, under circumstances which are familiar to my hon. friends, this government simply assumed its responsibility.
In a criminal case, the facts of which were brought to its attention, the federal government retained the services of outside legal counsel, who confirmed the advice of the legal advisers of the Department of Justice. Later on, the federal authorities lodged the required complaints in accord with the attorney general of the province. In so doing, the jurisdiction of the attorney general of the province was fully respected and proceedings were started and carried on jointly with the deputy crown attorney, whose authority is under the direct jurisdiction of the provincial attorney general of Quebec.
I also think that my hon. friend will agree with me that, when there is an injunction, according to articles 957 and following of the code of civil procedure, the jurisdiction with regard to intervention is entirely different.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to go into the Banks affair again at this time, except to say that I think the explanation of the Minister of Justice only tends to support what I said last night about Mr. Banks and the whole labour problem. The longer this unfortunate Banks affair goes on, the more the need for a federal labour code is demonstrated.
With regard to the amount of $700 million in interim supply, we certainly will have to go into some of the matters involved very carefully. First of all may I say I support the hon. member for Northwest Territories with regard to the Indian hospital situation in Alberta. I am not going to make any accusations but I do not like to see empire building. I do not mean British empire building. I do not like to see departmental empire building either in the province or in the do-

minion which will interfere with the welfare of our native people. I have about 6,500 of them in my own riding and therefore I think I have the right to speak on their behalf. They live under very primitive conditions, and I am very pleased that the hon. member for Northwest Territories, who has worked with these people, gave us a common sense viewpoint with regard to this whole matter, as he did this afternoon.
When these native people are under hospital care visiting is very important to them. Because they live in the wilds all their lives, perhaps they have something of the same feeling for territory as is found in wild animals. These people are close to the soil. I think it can be demonstrated by hospital charts indicating temperature, pulse rate and nervous condition that they are under continual stress when they are taken away from their native habitat to big cities. There is a very strong and cogent argument for the building of hospitals to look after these people as close to their homes as they can be built. I believe that such hospitals should be decentralized and that we should provide the best facilities we can in the north country where these people live.
The native people of the Northwest Territories and in Athabasca are increasing rapidly in numbers and therefore the need for hospitals will not diminish. Larger hospitals will be required in small, outlying areas. The only argument I can see in favour of taking these people to the city is that they may get better specialized care in the larger University hospital, or veterans hospital, but so far as on-site care is concerned these people can best be taken care of in the areas where they live, where they know the people and are more at home.
I have worked intimately with these people as an R.C.M.P. officer. I was responsible for the investigation of many welfare cases. We saw the worst ones, of course, but when we went into their homes and teepees we also saw a cross section of their needs. I would be the first to be opposed to anything like segregation. I do not suggest that we should segregate these people of the north in any way by building such hospitals. Quite the contrary. However, the provision of such hospitals means that the sick can be visited by their families.
Lest I should be misunderstood to be drawing some distinction between the white people and the native people of our country, may I say I do not think there is any such distinction except as to environment. I have

noticed on many occasions that so far as the sick are concerned there is much more distress among the older people. The older people who are used to the nomadic way of life are the ones who suffer most. When the children are taken away to hospital I believe they adjust much more rapidly. They tend to eat better and are more cheerful because they are better fed and clothed. They take to civilization and civilized surroundings much better. They do not suffer from the same nostalgia.
I suggest to the hon. lady that rather than spending $8i million to build this hospital in the wrong place the same amount of money should be spent to improve local facilities either by the provision of more beds in the Northwest Territories and the outlying districts of my own riding of Athabasca or by spending more money on drugs and services, transportation and communications. This suggestion may seem to be a little out of her field but I am quite sure it is important if you are going to provide these natives with proper treatment when they are sick.
You may be surprised, although you should not be, to know that in a great many cases these native people are not in touch with medical care of any kind. They are out in the woods or in encampments where there are no radio, telephone or telegraph facilities. I would suggest that in some cases it might be more important to run a telephone line to where these people are. Then first aid could be rendered on the spot rather than waiting until they develop pneumonia. There are many cases where children come down with a common cold, and because they are no longer clothed adequately in furs as they used to be they are subject to the danger of contracting tuberculosis or getting pneumonia. Then it is necessary to fly these people to the hospital at Edmonton at great expense.
Whether or not you are going to fly them to Edmonton, once communication is made and you know a native is sick another problem arises involving local transportation. In a great many cases there are no ambulances or snowmobiles located near where these people are living and in some cases the hospitals themselves do not have ambulances or snowmobiles to get to an Indian child or older Indian who needs hospital care.
I think some of this money might be spent for bursaries for social workers to encourage the training of more personnel. I think there should be an educational program among the people in the southern part of Canada to
Interim Supply
explain the need in outlying districts for trained social workers. Problems of this sort are all of a piece. One of the difficulties that the hon. lady will run into, and I think she has encountered it already, is the need for nurses. That naturally leads to the next question. What are we going to do about nurses? Some two or three years ago I brought up the question of what we could do about obtaining more nurses. I did some research in this matter and I suggested that the reason we were thousands of nurses short in Canada was that we were taking a very unrealistic and non-20th century approach to the whole question of nursing.
I communicated with the Canadian nurses' association, and what did I get? No doubt they are well meaning people, but they are living in the mental atmosphere of Florence Nightingale. I received a very irate letter from the president of this association, no doubt a trained nurse with many years of service. She wrote to me and said that if we gave these young nursing students a dollar a day pocket money in order to go to a picture show or buy nylons, we would be putting out the lamp of Florence Nightingale. She said that these girls were looking after serious cases, deadly dangerous cases. I do not need to go into the details, because you can imagine them for yourselves. There would be people with cancer of the bowel and all sorts of diseases. You have a young girl just out of school working under very difficult conditions. This woman wrote to me-I am not going to name her-and said that if we gave this young girl a dollar a day we would be putting out the lamp of Florence Nightingale. I do not believe that this is so at all.
There are many young girls who come in off the farm whose parents are unable to support them, and a dollar a day is not too much to pay them for this work. If there are any young girls entering this course who are so altruistic they believe they should not receive this $1 a day, this miserable $1, then they can donate it to the crippled children's society or the Red Cross. There are many of these young girls who want to go into training as nurses but they are too proud to ask their parents to support them for three years. They have no means of supporting themselves during these years and many of them, after spending some years, wish they had chosen some other profession which would at least allow them to buy their own nylons and go to the picture show.

The situation is so desperate these young nurses are talking about being unionized. I do not blame them. Surely, we do not have to drive them to the point of being unionized. We do not have to get to the point where these girls have to bring in people like Hoffa and Banks to organize them in order that they might receive the treatment you would expect for your daughter.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that the topic with which he is dealing, namely the training and organizing of nurses, is in the provincial field of jurisdiction and has nothing to do with the estimates now before the house?

I suggest that it should be in the estimates before the committee. I brought this matter up with the former administration. It got to the point where it was being considered by the cabinet. They were considering putting a resolution through as part of the health and welfare estimates. This scheme was frustrated by the nursing profession. You can just leave it there if you want it that way and say, all right, if the president of the nursing profession is speaking for all the young nurses in Canada, then that is what we will do. I assure you she does not speak for these young nurses because my file is full of letters from young nurses all across Canada. This one letter apparently frustrated the idea of giving encouragement to nurses in training in Canada.
I think there is no doubt at all that nurses may well be included in this very vague Bill No. C-110. There is no reference to nurses in the bill, but I asked if they were included and I received a very evasive answer. I believe that any young person in Canada who was expecting some kind of bursary or some kind of loan is to be given encouragement. I believe the provisions of this bill were wide and would include everybody. I am asking the minister, who is in charge of health throughout Canada, to use her good offices to press this point. I was not successful in pushing it through the former administration. I had a most encouraging hearing from the then minister of national health and welfare and, as I said, the subject was being considered by the government. Apparently the idea was frustrated by the members of the nursing profession themselves.

I think this is a shortsighted, narrow view within the nursing profession. I believe it is preventing the recruiting of these nurses which we need so badly. Everybody who has been in hopsital in recent years knows the hospitals are being filled with nurses aides. Everybody knows this is only a stopgap. At one time I believe we had nearly enough nurses to look after the number of beds we had. We are so short of nurses today that we have to bring in untrained girls, pay them $200 or $300 a month to do the very work these nursing students are required to do. They are washing the facilities, you know, and they are scrubbing the floors. They are doing the sort of work they have always done. However because we are short of nurses we bring in nurses aides to do the same work.
Another argument that has been put up by those who do not want to spend money sensibly is that these student nurses are on the job training. When they complete their training, they will be in the professional class. All right, when you join the mounted police as a recruit you are on the job training. Our officers contend that a recruit is absolutely useless to them, in fact he is a detriment. During the first year they are spending all their time getting him used to the saddle, how to handle a rifle, and so on. However, at the present time he gets something like $250 in starting pay and I think that is the way it should be. You will get your value out of him before he completes 25 years in that noble service. Why should nurses not be doing the same thing as other people?
We have lots of people now who are ready to take up the cudgels, and I am one of them, in favour of these young people, these fine young girls, who want to go through to be nurses and have their life of dedicated service. I do not believe that the fact we pay them $300 a month, after they are trained at the end of three years of hard work, necessarily pays them back for everything they have done. A good nurse is priceless. You cannot buy this kind of help. The mere fact that they are dedicated is absolutely no excuse for saying that if you give them a miserable dollar a day they are going to put out the lamp. If that is the kind of lamp we have burning in Canada today, we had better put out that lamp and put another lamp of common sense in there to make sure these girls receive justice. I should like the hon. lady to see my file on this subject. It is quite impressive. If she did, I think she would agree that something should be done.

Then, I should like to consider the patient. I know that if I were a patient seriously ill, knowing that I require my temperature to be taken, I would feel much better if I could see the cap of the trained nurse. Nurses aides are all right because they do the bullwork, but I like to see as many trained nurses as possible when I am sick. My health is important to me. When my wife is sick, it is far more important to me. I have investigated enough hospitals to know that today many hospitals are not equipped with the proper number of professional personnel. If this is the result of niggardliness, I think we are doing it in the wrong place. If we are going to pick on the nursing students, I think that is the wrong place. As I said, I am inclined to think that the graduate nurse herself today is not in agreement with the policy of training. This brings up a matter which I should like to mention, and I am not trying to be critical. I am trying to look to the future. I suggest there may be an answer, and the question of framing-

partment of health. I propose that a new department be set up, to be known as the department of youth-

At the present time, with the population explosion and the coming of automation, this problem of looking after our youth is far too big for any small group within any one department, and in nearly every department of government we already have existing services for the training of youth. My friends in the comer are not my trained seals, and there is really no need for all this slapping and banging down there.

It is obvious that there is a need for juvenile training. Some of the hon. mem-

bers have apparently reached a mature age and a certain physical stature, and I do not propose to give them a lecture on their manners; I expect the minimum.

In regard to the matter of juvenile delinquency, I suppose the minister might say this is a matter for the justice department, and so it has been up to date. I beg the attention of the members of the committee. I think our youth deserve this attention. I hope they will listen to me with the same attention that I will listen to them. The fact is that throughout this whole debate they have chosen to abdicate their position as members of the opposition. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

I thank them for their applause. If they have not the courage or the interest in our young people to get up and say it themselves, there is nothing I appreciate more than their wholehearted support. But I beg them again to withhold their applause, because before I have finished my remarks they will not perhaps be in such a receptive mood.
Hear, hear.

1 would like to charge this department with the responsibility of assisting in a nation-wide program for citizenship training. Citizenship starts with health. Without a very high standard of national health it is difficult to be good citizens, in the true sense. I think a great deal more attention should be paid to this question and more plant should be developed. We are desperately short of facilities for juvenile training in the matter of sports and physical fitness. There are many people in this country who do not want regimentation of any kind. Neither do I. But there are a good many people who are willing to donate their time and talents to such a program if we have the plant and recreational facilities. Many individuals and service groups are willing to co-operate to the fullest extent, but the problem is so large at the present time that I suggest it is time we took on such a program as a national project. Knowing the interest the present minister has taken from one end of her department to the other in the matter of national health, I know her hands are full with the pension plan, aid to the provinces and many of the other projects which are under way in her department. I would suggest, therefore, that she get together with her cabinet colleagues and put forward this suggestion.
Hear, hear.

It is nothing new; but nothing definite has been done on it so far. I hope the other members of the committee who have an interest in the young people of our country will at least give me their moral support.

Mr. Chairman, after having listened to the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg), I should like to refute his arguments one after the other. I see the hon. member is making gestures.
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. [Text]

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Saskatoon on her maiden speech in this house. She pointed out the plight of the mentally ill and geriatric patient. Truly, the saddest hours in anyone's life must be those spent as a geriatric mental patient. She also pointed to the necessity of having patients annexed to a general hospital where they can be treated by a general practitioner for their physical illness and by a psychiatrist for their mental condition.
Interim Supply
Hear, hear.

One difficulty in carrying out this program is that we have not got the beds. We have not got the accommodation close enough to the general hospitals. Above all, as she so well demonstrated, we have not got the personnel and the psychiatrists to put this plan into effect.
The minister of health and welfare heads a department which is the second highest spending department in the government.
Hear, hear.

All of our vast social security plans under the federal government are administered by her department. The Canada pension plan, which is now plan four, will be under her care-or will it?
I should just like to say that this plan must have as its target the care of those who are in need and who have reached the age of retirement or the age where they cannot work any longer no matter what their age. The wealthy and the well-to-do are not likely to need this pension. Indeed the fear which I think must be felt by us all, as the government channels more and more money into its coffers through hospitalization costs, pension plans, unemployment insurance, municipal, provincial and federal taxes, is that the working man, if he apportions it generally, will be left with just enough to buy his food, his clothes and his shelter. This can reach the point where the government will control all investments in the country and direct the persons whose liberty they have nibbled away at over the years under the guise of paternalism.
In the year and a half that this government has been in power what has happened? The first thing they did was to increase income taxes. The second thing was to impose an escalating sales tax of 11 per cent on building materials and equipment. And third, they brought about an almost monthly rise in the cost of living. I am just pointing this out, Mr. Chairman, because it is of concern to us all. If this condition continues and the government keep channelling more and more of the people's earned dollars into government funds, then we will soon become the pawns of the state.
I would be interested in knowing what progress the minister has made in the field of the control of cigarette smoking by our young people at school. I should like to congratulate her on setting an example to our young boys and girls as well as to their

Interim Supply
parents in the steps she has taken. But has she any indication what has been the impact of her plan on the young people at school? How much has been spent of the $600,000 provided? The minister has had her department write a book. I want to compliment her on that book because it is a better book than some of the books written by other ministers. It is a very good book on the dangers of cigarette smoking. What has been the progress made by this book in educating teenagers against the dangers of smoking? What combined oifensive has the government made with the provincial departments of health? Has the story been made impressive enough? Each and every day seven people die in Canada of cancer of the lung. This amounts to 2,500 people per year, which is more than those killed in traffic accidents. Cigarettes are a major cause of cancer of the lung, but how many of our boys and girls across the land have read the minister's book? How many of the 450 boys and girls between the ages of 11 and 17 who start smoking every day have read this book? This matter is of vital concern to every home and to every boy and girl. As the president of the Canadian medical association remarked, several factors play a part in cancer of the lung, including air pollution, but the most important factor of all is cigarette smoking.
Cigarette smoking per capita has tripled in the last 20 years. This is an amazing thing when we consider how cancer of the lung has increased so rapidly, faster than any other cancer in the body. Doctor Best of the department of health reported in a six year study of the smoking habits of 78,000 war veterans of the first great war, the second great war and the Korean war that the cause of death of these veterans was as follows. Four hundred and fifty four smokers died of lung cancer compared with every 100 nonsmokers. Thirty nine per cent of these veterans died from coronary artery disease and 47 per cent died from other heart and circulatory disease. For persons over 30 who smoked cigarettes only the death rate was 52 per cent higher. Surely no further argument is needed.
I would ask the minister whether she is satisfied that she is doing everything she should. Is she satisfied that her budget of $600,000 is enough? How much of this figure has she spent? Is the minister satisfied with supporting the tobacco grower of cigarette tobacco, or is it better to encourage cigar and pipe tobacco smoking or chewing tobacco

growers, and to discourage the cultivation of cigarette tobacco? I wonder. Cigarettes are the worst offender in cancer of the lung. I think this is worth thinking about because the manufacturers of cigarettes have not done enough research to prove what is the carcinogenic material in cigarettes. Therefore, 1 think it behooves us, if people are going to continue to smoke, to switch them into the tobacco, which will not have such a deleterious effect as cigarettes, such as cigar smoking, pipe smoking and, if you want, chewing tobacco. I think we should consider this very seriously as grown up adults, and not in a political way.
Has the minister considered any plan to control cigarette advertising? Tobacco companies on the North American continent spend $150 million on advertising each year. They do this in the hope of selling more of their product or having people switch to another brand. Otherwise they would not spend the money. Has the minister or her department considered the printing of a warning on every package of cigarettes? I do not know whether the minister is listening. Generally she is fairly attentive.
She is not interested.

She does not appear to be interested but this comes under her department. I say again: Has the minister considered the printing of a warning on cigarette packages? This comes under her department and she should be considering it.
I should also like to ask the minister if she has considered setting up a committee to check on cigarette advertising. In the United States they have agreed to appoint a controller of advertising. I suggest to the minister that it would be good business for her and her department to consider the same sort of control.
I feel the problem is a very serious one in that the boys and girls who are going to school should be kept from smoking cigarettes. I wonder whether we are doing all we can to enforce the law. I am wondering about the cigarette vending machines where you put in your money, push a little button and a package of cigarettes comes out. What is to prevent a boy or girl under 16 getting cigarettes from such a vending machine? What has the department done about that? Is it sincere about the program or is it just paying lipservice to it?
If my memory serves me correctly, a survey made in the province of Saskatchewan

indicated that 50 per cent of the boys attending high school smoked and 33J per cent of the girls.
Hear, hear.

If some of us are not concerned about the deleterious and fatal effects of cancer of the lung I think we should be most concerned from an economic point of view, because it has been proved over and over again that the boys and girls who start smoking in high school have the worst academic records. I say that this is costing the country a lot of money.
We have also been told that the government is studying the Hall royal commission report and is going to bring in its recommendations very soon. I would remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the government that in less than 10 years from now, 1970, we will be short 7,000 doctors in the Dominion of Canada. I have stated this before but the problem is very serious. This information is found in the Hall commission report.
The hon. member for Saskatoon ably pointed out the mess we are in today because of the lack of trained personnel in the field of psychiatry, and the same condition is rapidly developing in the field of medicine generally. The Hall commission report also points out that we will need five new medical schools. I say to the government that before they can implement the report of the commission the federal government or the provincial governments must get busy and build more medical schools and universities. If we do not have the buildings we cannot train the young men and women of this country as doctors dentists, nurses and scientists.
Hear, hear.

This is one of the very pressing problems facing the Department of National Health and Welfare today. If my memory serves me correctly, I believe we raised the per capita grant from $1 to $2, when we were in power. The minister is watching me and if I am wrong I know I will be corrected. I suggest to the department that the per capita grant be doubled again because of the pressing need for more university buildings. I see the hon. member for Kingston is listening and I am sure he will agree, in view of the program and the needs of Queen's University.
In my own riding of Simcoe East there is a radar station that is being closed down. The buildings and grounds cost approximately $9 million but they are now in the hands of

Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. In view of the report of the Hall commission and in view of what we know about the situation in respect of education, I think it would be one of the finest things the federal government could do if it would make a grant sufficient to establish a university there. The buildings and the site are available. All the government has to do is to make the necessary grant to get the personnel so that a university can be established. I am sure the provincial government would gladly receive the grant.
Once again I reiterate that time is running out, because 1970 is less than 10 years away when we will need all these trained personnel.
Hear, hear.

We have been getting them from Europe and Great Britain and we will still need these people very badly in the next few years until we turn out the necessary graduates. Remember that it takes seven years from the time a doctor starts until he graduates. This is the real problem. You cannot start today and graduate tomorrow. Time is running out on us. We have a problem right now which has existed for some time but it is becoming more acute. All one has to do is read the daily press to learn how hard pressed most doctors are today.
So I say to the government that even before they consider the Hall commission report they must deal with this matter as one of very great urgency because how can they consider a plan when they do not have the personnel? We have got to have universities. We have got to have the buildings and equipment. We must have the trained personnel. To my mind this makes sense.
Hear, hear.

The time is late and the matter is urgent. Again I ask the minister to keep in mind some of the R.C.A.F. stations that are being abandoned because the air force has no further use for them. I ask the minister to look at them very carefully to see if they cannot be utilized for the training of the young men and young women we need so badly in the professional world. I want to thank my friends to the left for their applause.

Mr. Chairman, I would be remiss at this time if I did not extend my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Saskatoon on the occasion of her maiden speech in the house. I know how she must have felt because it is not too long ago that I had the same experience. At that time my legs were shaking badly and my knees were

Interim Supply
knocking. But the hon. member tor Saskatoon made an outstanding contribution to the debate and I think she should be congratulated by every member in the house on this occasion.
I seize this opportunity to say a few words on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Actually, time does not mean anything anyway. It is quite apparent we are going to sit here all summer.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if this house is going to spend the next two hours listening to the kind of organized heckling which we have had. Surely the members who want to speak have a right to speak while order is maintained. We sat here last week while the members of this group put on the record their opinions of the students loan fund, whether it was constitutional or whether it infringed the rights of the people of Quebec. Nobody interfered with them. Nobody questioned their right to speak. I appeal to you-I think it is useless to appeal to them or to their common sense and judgment-to exercise the authority which you have. Let us have a little order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to speak to the point of order because I had similar trouble with the members of the Creditiste party last week, particularly the hon. member for Lapointe. I draw your attention, sir, to standing order 59, paragraph (4) which reads:
The chairman shall maintain order in the committees of the whole house, deciding all questions of order subject to an appeal to the house; hut disorder in a committee can only be censured by the house, on receiving a report thereof.
I think, sir, that gives you the necessary authority that is required to restrain this type of interruption, which is simply disorder.
I should like to have the floor again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Hon. members who take part in a debate in the committee are entitled to be heard without interruption from other hon. members in the committee. Hon. members will realize this and will want to cooperate with the Chair. I therefore appeal to members in the committee to be fair in this way and allow their colleagues a chance to be heard quietly.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on the point of order.

You have certainly noticed that we have often applauded from the very beginning. In fact, we have applauded when the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) mentioned that tobacco was dangerous. We have also applauded when someone pointed out what the minister should do, because we felt that those were proper suggestions. We applauded when the hon. member who now has the floor said that we were going to sit all summer, because we feel that this makes sense.
I wonder why the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) should wish to prevent us from showing our approval when we feel that certain remarks are appropriate.
Besides that, I cannot see what trouble we may have caused. I have been in this house for two years and I did not know that applause was not allowed.
When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) speaks, all Conservatives without exception applaud, even if what he says means nothing.
When an hon. member makes remarks which are meaningful and is applauded, we should not be accused of causing disorder; on the contrary, we approve him.
Therefore, why complain?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sure the hon. member for Lapointe understands very well the point raised by the members objecting to the applause, too prolonged perhaps, for some of their colleagues, and I ask him to cooperate with the Chair in order to allow the hon. member who has the floor to continue his remarks without interruption.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate very much your remarks. I know that you are not going to penalize me for the time of which I have been robbed. I should like to say that I do not know why the hon. member for Lapointe would say he would be willing to sit here all summer because he has not sat during any part of the session. He has had springs in his posterior. He has been up and down like a jack-in-the-box. I should like to say also that these trained seals we have-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.
The hon. member who now has the floor just stated that I have not taken part in the debates of the house from my seat. One must

be really impudent to say such a thing because, if he referred to Hansard, he would see that I have been here every day. Besides, when he rose to speak, I said to one of my colleagues: "Where has this one been all the time; is he a new member?" I tell you quite frankly, Mr. Chairman, that neither I nor my colleagues have ever seen him. It takes some cheek to make such a statement.

As I say, I do not mind the trained seals getting up and kind of flapping their flippers a little bit, but I wish they would improve their sense of rhythm, because they are out of metre. They are putting the punctuation marks in the wrong places in my speech. I know they will co-operate with me, and I appreciate that very much.
As I was saying a moment ago, time does not actually mean too much because we are going to be here all summer. So far as I am concerned, I am satisfied if we sit here until Christmas. We have a lot of work to do, and let us get along with it. I should like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare if she feels this is actually in the best interest of the health and welfare of the members if we do sit all summer and fall.
Last night I referred to one of the ministers who has co-operated with me a great deal. There are other ministers who have done the same thing. I am very pleased with that experience of being able to do some business with them. However I did have occasion some time ago, as a result of a phone call which I received from the city clerk of the city of London, to try to obtain a reference from the Minister of National Health and Welfare for a man who was making application for the position of assistant city solicitor. Now, I did go to the minister because the man in question had worked in her office for five years. I shall not dilate too much on the reference that was given, but I will say that the adjectives that were used were actually something to behold. They were far from complimentary. I am asking this question: Why did she keep him for five years? Was the report I received a personal report, and if so how personal was it? It does illustrate one of two things, Mr. Chairman-either a great amount of vindictiveness or a lack of administrative and executive ability. I am asking, Mr. Chairman, is this the kind of person who should head up such an important portfolio as that of health, welfare and truth? This department is today working on a budget of something like $700 million.
Interim Supply
I should like also to say something tonight with regard to, I was going to say, the Canada pension plan but, perhaps I should say a Canada pension plan, because we have had so many of them. The first one that was introduced, you will recall, resulted in the province of Quebec opting out, and it was taken back. Then, at the time of the introduction of the next plan the premier of Ontario objected, I think after much provocation, and refused to deal with the minister. I am wondering, Mr. Chairman, just what we do at this point. It is quite apparent that at that time the Prime Minister stepped in and perhaps assumed a great deal of responsibility. To whom do we turn now? Do we still deal with the Prime Minister or has the Minister of National Health and Welfare been reinstated? People want to get along with this plan. There are many people in this country who are interested in this plan and they would like to get along with the introduction of it. We know that there are constitutional amendments that are necessary. Perhaps if this had been properly researched in the first place, the constitutional amendment might have been secured before the plan was presented to the house.
I should also like to say a word about blind pensions. This is assistance for those people who live in a world of darkness, people who have a special cross of their own to bear. They should receive some sort of special treatment. In most cases when a person who is blind goes outside his own domicile he must have someone to go along with him. This is a necessity, and in many cases a costly necessity. If he goes downtown, or to the centre of the area where he lives, he must go by bus or other special public transportation, and this is an extra cost.
Further, because of their infirmity, blind people are not able to read the advertisements in their local papers so that they can take advantage of the specials advertised and thus save money on their purchases. For these and many other reasons I think there should be a very definite and immediate review of their allowances.
I have a copy of a magazine published by the Confederation of the Blind, Inc., called "Vision". It is the 1964 summer issue, volume 19, No. 2 and I should like to quote some of the resolutions passed by the Canadian Federation of the Blind in convention assembled on June 23, 1964:
Therefore be it resolved that the Canadian Federation of the Blind continue to ask the dominion government to increase the blind pension from $75 per month to $85 per month for every blind person.

Therefore be it resolved that the Canadian Federation of the Blind continue to press the provincial governments for a school to be established in the province of Saskatchewan as soon as possible.
I think we might help in this. It is very important work. The magazine goes on to say:
Therefore be it resolved that the means test at present in effect on the government pension to the blind be removed, permitting a blindness allowance to be paid to all blind persons.
The final item I would like to read is this:
Be it resolved that the Canadian Federation of the Blind urge the government of Canada to abolish the means test at present in effect on the pension to the blind so that it shall be paid to all blind persons as the allowance recommended by the world council for the welfare of the blind.
I think we might even expand on this a little further, and if necessary we could go to the department and do a little checking, cut out a great deal of the waste, and place some of the money in the places where it is needed so badly.
With regard to the disabled persons allowances, they need assistance because of the rising cost of living, just as the blind people need assistance. These are things which the department should be considering, and in addition there is the assistance to our senior citizens. I have with me a copy of a letter from Fort Macleod, Alberta, which I think all hon. members received, and I would like to quote a portion of it:
-the pensioners and senior citizens go on record as extending a sincere thanks for all that has been done and hope further assistance is forthcoming.
Whereas a couple in receipt of old age pension and death strikes, leaving a burden on the survivor for debts incurred; be it resolved that the pension of the deceased be continued for a period of six months.
Whereas the price of drugs and medical prescriptions are generally too high for pensioners and others of low income and appear to the lay mind exorbitant; be it resolved that we ask for an impartial government inquiry as to whether such prices are justified or necessary, and if found to be so, whether some system could be devised whereby they could be made available, free when necessary, to those below income tax level.
Further they state, and I am not necessarily recommending this except for study, that the old age security pension be given at age 65 and that old age assistance be given at age 60. The letter goes on to say:
Resolved that old age security pension be increased to $85 per month. However, we consider

that, whereas the cost of living has been, and continues to rise and whereas a contributory old age security contributory scheme is in the offing; therefore be it enacted that the old age security monthly pension be raised by $5 each year until a pension of $100 monthly is reached. Why not mark Canada's centennial year by reaching that $100 by the 100th celebration of existence of our country?
I could go on at great length dealing with numerous people who need assistance. In many cases they will not come to us but I think we should go to them and protect them because they need the protection we are in a position to give them.
There are the retarded children, and these embrace a great group of people. There are about half a million retarded children in Canada-and I am not including the people in the far corner of this chamber. This half million directly affect approximately another one million people in their families. I have here a letter which I received from the secretary of the London branch of the Canadian association for retarded children, wherein she says this:
In the proposal you will note we have referred to the fact that the C.N.I.B. already receives a $50,000 grant from the federal government for support in its program, yet mental retardation ranks first among the chronic disabilities of childhood. Socially it is the most serious problem in respect of the number affected and its effect on the lives of all those closely involved with the problem.
I realize that the government is watching its spending very closely but surely if it can find $600,000 to support a preventive program on smoking it can afford the $65,000 the Canadian association for retarded children has requested in this proposal.
Finally I would point out to you that, as a result of the magnitude of this problem approximately one in nine people in your constituency are affected in their attempts to develop community facilities for the retarded of all ages.
I think the amount they ask, only $65,000, is a pitifully small amount when you consider how worthy the cause is and I suggest to the minister, when she gets through reading the paper, that she take a look at this letter.
There are so many areas in this department and we waste so much money that it seems to me with good business methods we could cut and pare a little bit of waste, and find enough money to provide this assistance for retarded children.
I would like to say in conclusion-
Hear, hear.

You know, Mr. Chairman, it is very odd that when people retire for dinner they get tied up with a mixture of south wind and rainwater and react very strangely.

With great respect for the people in the department I say there is so little completed and so much to be done that I shall sit down so that the minister can finally start to work.

There have been many interesting and apt comments made about the Department of National Health and Welfare this afternoon. Since the department in question is the second largest spending department in the government, I certainly think it is legitimate for the committee to spend a few hours of its time examining some of the expenditures proposed or to be made by this important department. We have had no other opportunity to examine them and many of us have been anxious to discuss some of the interesting and important programs which come within the minister's purview.
The annual report put out by the department makes interesting reading and touches on a wide field of activities which affect every single Canadian be he young or old, active or retired, sick or well. This being the case, the department has been able to provide some interesting and necessary measures to improve the lives of the people to whom they are directed. I was very interested, as were other members of this committee, in the address given by the hon. member for Saskatoon. I thought her learned dissertation served as an example of application to government business which we would do well to follow. The hon. lady pointed out that improved facilities and increases in competent professional staff have much to do with the efficacy of services, and I share her view in this regard. While these improvements seem to call for an increase in expenditure, the greater response which follows from improved care enables patients to get back much earlier to a productive role in the community than would otherwise be the case, so that they can once again take their place side by side with those who are paying income tax and helping to provide for these medical services.
Though we talk about the large sums spent by this department, we are not saying they are too large. We simply want the right and the privilege to suggest how this money might best be applied. This is what we have been doing this afternoon and there have been some interesting comments about the activities of this important department. The hon. member for Saskatoon mentioned the benefits which have followed the use of sheltered workshops-how they have helped in the convalescence of the mentally ill. I believe
Interim Supply
this system could be extended and, indeed, it has been extended to others such as the mentally retarded, the physically handicapped, blind and other disabled persons who are unable to compete on today's competitive labour market in the absence of some special provision which makes it possible for them to gain a livelihood.
This brings up the question of increased grants toward the maintenance of these facilities. While many grants are being increased year by year it seems we still have to persuade government and society-persuade ourselves, really-that this is a good investment; that it is, in the long term, a saving because it will mean a return to a useful life so much earlier of a great many people who are at present in need of assistance.
The hon. member for the Northwest Territories showed that savings amounting to more than $8 million could be made by the proper location of hospitals and he gave some logical reasons why this should be done. These are some of the things which have been said this afternoon. I wanted to follow them up and to preface the second part of my remarks by saying it is important we have the right attitudes in this house, in this country, and in society generally so that we may work out the kind of legislation which will be most useful to the people it is designed to benefit.
I was very pleased to take part in the conference on the family which was held at Rideau Hall earlier this summer. On June 7, deeply moving ceremonies took place at Government House at which there were warm expressions of gratitude to Governor General and Madame Vanier for having inspired the conference and brought it to life. I hope this conference will become a useful legacy to Canada in the same way as other legacies have been left to us by governors general of days gone by-and I think, in passing, of the Victorian Order of Nurses, the Grey cup and Massey hall, to mention only a few of the legacies which have been left to us by the highest officials of the land.
For three days, some 300 highly qualified and competent persons from a wide range of disciplines discussed matters not specifically directed to welfare activities alone, but concerning, nevertheless, the well-being of the family. Such matters as health and welfare, education, income, community planning and family stability were discussed and some of the generalized conclusions we often reach about such matters were brought into question and received some scientific testing. I was

Interim Supply
very interested, for example, to hear views on the effect of mobility on the stability of family life. We often hear it said that it is this restlessness, this mobility which has been an important factor in loosening family ties. But I was reminded at the conference that when our grandparents moved from the rural areas to the cities, perhaps a distance of only 150 miles, they might as well have crossed an ocean, such was the lack of communication facilities at that time. I was also reminded that within only a 60 year period, or perhaps somewhat longer, the prairies of Manitoba and other western parts of Canada were being put to the plow by families from the British Isles, the Ukraine and other European countries. This all involved the movement of people, yet it did not assist toward the destruction of family life.
Thus, I question the simple diagnosis that the disintegration of family life today has come about because we move around so much. In fact, these people of migrant stock, established in so many communities, did much for Canadian culture by bringing with them their European traditions and sense of individuality. Many generations have been raised and have grown up in the same community as those in which their grandparents lived. To a certain extent, this provided for them a measure of security. On the other hand many families did not move away, simply because they were never able to do so; they were not making an adequate living where they were, and they never had the funds to make it possible to move elsewhere. In this connection I am interested to see how the program sponsored by the Minister of Industry will work out- the program to relocate people who live in areas of chronic unemployment.
I think it is appropriate to call to the attention of the committee the message delivered by the Governor General to the conference on the family because I believe that the success of any legislation depends on proper attitude toward the national need. The Governor General phrased this in an excellent way in the statement he made at the conference and I will read his words from the June issue of the publication Canadian Welfare put out by the Canadian Welfare Council.
Many years of observation, experience and study have convinced my wife and me that happy and united families make a happy and united community and thus constitute an essential element of peace in our world.
The family, although a unit small in size, is the most important of all, because upon it depends the future of mankind. The role of the family

is not limited merely to the physical existence of future generations but extends to moral and spiritual considerations as well. Parents, united by ties of affection and devoid of self-interest, are the first to open the hearts and minds of children to the values of the spirit, values of truth, justice and religion. The parents plant the first seeds of love, generosity and selflessness and thus fashion and guide youth on the way to becoming citizens devoted to noble causes for the common good.
Unfortunately our time, for the young, is one of confusion and disorder in which the state of the family is sadly threatened, but it is not without hope. There is an elite of thinkers and of social workers struggling, with intelligence and devotion, with the problems of our society. There is an elite of parents and educators earnestly striving to hearten and inspire youth. Is it not worth while, then, that men and women of good will should meet and exchange ideas and experiences, that they should together examine the special difficulties of the family in this modem age?
I quote this because I think it is very appropriate to the discussion on any of the measures of the Department of National Health and Welfare, because these great expenditures are and have been made necessary because of the ills that have crept into our way of life. We are spending moneys, and therefore we need to understand why it is becoming necessary to spend moneys. What do we pay, for example, for unemployment? It has been said, and we know from statistics, that an average of 6 or 7 per cent of the labour force has been unemployed in recent years. With this kind of drop in employment our productivity naturally also decreases. It has been estimated that in the last two or three years this lack of employment, or this decrease in productivity, has cost the country between $2| billion and $3 billion in terms of the decline in the gross national product. This is a price we have paid-and we cannot retrieve it-to say nothing of the human qualities that accompany unemployment, the loss of dignity, lack of happiness, lack of fulfilment, and so forth.
What do we pay for sickness? This is very hard to tabulate, because enormous amounts of money are spent at the municipal level, the provincial level and the federal level, in addition to the moneys paid out by the individuals themselves. Again, the price is enormous. We paid it last year and the year before, and we will pay it again. Is it not fair to ask: Are we spending this money in the most equitable manner possible. What is the cost of lack of education? There are a host of things that could be listed here. There is the cost to the individual and the cost to society. To the individual it often

means less employment possibilities, lack of self-realization and often long periods of existence on welfare benefits and the like. To society it has greater implications, this lack of proper education with the proper attitudes that go with it. For one thing the lack of a widely based education can produce shortsighted and ineffective government policies. It has been said that many causes have contributed to delinquency, but certainly lack of education is one of these. One of the other results of ignorance or lack of education is the manner in which newspapers devote so much space to the sensational reporting of crime. If we were not so anxious to read these sensational reports, the newspapers would not want to publish them; but we seem to want them and therefore the newspapers give them to us. It is reflected in another area of our life, and that is the jukeboxes and radios blaring out a cacophony of primitive noises that raise doubts whether civilization is advancing at all. It is reflected in a surfeit of phony westerns, cops and robbers and spurious medics that have made a wasteland of television. The hon. member for Athabasca mentioned modern art as coming into this category.
These are the costs of lack of education, of informed thought, and these costs are inescapable. Against such costs the price of education seems ridiculously low. In these areas, then, we have no choice about paying, because we have already paid and will have to pay again; but we certainly have a large element of choice as to how we shall continue to pay. If we are wise we shall pay for improved education, health and welfare and similar services simply because we cannot afford ignorance, we cannot afford sickness and we cannot afford personal misery. We must learn therefore to pay for positive and preventive measures, rather than for negative and only remedial actions. For this reason I believe conferences such as the one sponsored by the Governor General will develop the kind of attitude, the kind of thought, the kind of co-ordinated promotion that might yet bring about the measures we so badly need.
All these areas, ignorance, sickness, poverty and crime are inter-related and react to each other. The proverb "Many are the handmaidens of poverty" is so true. There is a great need for closer integration of the efforts of all the helping professions and organizations. A beginning was made with the conference on the family, where these different professions did meet together. When I
Interim Supply
was asked what I felt was the outcome of this conference I said that the biggest accomplishment was the fact that it was being held. This is a beginning, and a step in the right direction.
The dark spectre of poverty seems to hang behind many of the needs and programs that the department has to administer. A best selling book about poverty in the United States and a recent C.B.C. television program on the series "Horizon" called "Another Canada" have made us all aware that poverty does haunt this land. The "Horizon" program used figures from the dominion bureau of statistics to show that a minimum of 3 million persons in Canada are poor, and as a general, rough guideline they defined poor in this way; in the city, families who have an income of less than $2,500 per year, and in the rural areas families that have an income of $1,200 or less per year. It has been stated that this is a minimum figure and some estimates go as high as 5 million people in Canada who live at this marginal level of existence. I think this is a regrettable development in this affluent country, and we really are not concerned enough about this because the people for the most part are invisible. Yet they are Canadians and fellow citizens. We must provide measures that will improve their lot. Thus we will really improve the lot of everyone in the country, because they can become much more useful to society if they can be made part of it, not only by giving them employment but by making them feel they belong to the society also.
Lack of motivation, lack of hope and incentive is a more subtle but no less formidable barrier than lack of financial needs. This is so often the case with people who have not had the opportunities to develop and reach their full potential. Poverty breeds poverty, and this is an endless cycle. Unless somewhere someone can break the cycle, I think recommendations such as those coming out of the Hall commission report give us some clue as to how we can break this cycle. The fact that health services are being recommended for all, regardless of ability to pay, is very necessary because many times it is lack of adequate health standards that puts a person in a position where he cannot remain employed or cannot reach his full potential in school, or where his parents are limited, for financial reasons, in providing those health measures that are so necessary for all of us. I think the Hall commission report gives us some guidelines and I am hopeful that the

Interim Supply
government will find an early opportunity to implement this report.
While speaking about the Hall commission report, I want to make reference to a lesser recommendation because I am sure other hon. members will give fuller treatment to this report. One of the recommendations is that the administration of health services for Indians and Eskimos should be entrusted to the provinces, and health services should be provided in the same manner and in the same quality as those enjoyed by other Canadians. I want to really emphasize this because at the present time there seems to be a double standard. There are many situations in which, just because a person is an Indian there is a division in the type of service offered at the present time. Not too long ago I asked question No. 1,405 of the minister, and this question was answered last Monday. I asked the minister whether or not Indian children in Winnipeg or other centres, who for medical reasons were placed in foster homes, were placed in licensed homes in accordance with local child care standards. The answer given was that some of the homes so used are licensed by the city of Winnipeg as boarding homes for children. The answer went on:
However the city health regulations do not require licensing of homes caring for less than three children at a time. It is not departmental practice to place more than two children in any one home at any one time.
It is with this answer that I want to quarrel with the minister, because I do not understand how it is that the city of Winnipeg health regulations with regard to Indian children would be different from those concerning the placement of other children. I know from my own experience that a child placed in a foster home must be placed in a home with a boarding permit, and if this answer is correct I am anxious to know why this is not required with Indian children. The specific situation which prompted this question arose from a case where neighbours had been complaining of the maltreatment of Indian children in a specific foster home. Therefore I would ask that the situation be looked into, because I shudder to think of children being brought to a centre for medical attention because they have been mistreated by improperly supervised foster parents who may not have the children's welfare at heart but perhaps only the fee provided for their services.
I do not wish to malign foster parents in general because I have the highest regard for people who are able to function in this way. These people are able to give of themselves to
[Mr. Enns.f
other people's children; they are able to take them into their homes and their hearts. I think they are the kind of people who have a special place in our society and perhaps in heaven, for that matter, because few of us could perform the service that foster parents provide. But there are those not properly screened who do not have this facility and actually do damage to such children. It is for this reason that I show concern over this double standard in the area of health services as between Indians and Eskimos and the rest of our Canadian children. That these are difficult and even baffling times is true; but they are not times for despair but for informed, forthright and purposeful decisions. Is this too much to expect from the present government?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add my words of congratulation to those which have already been said to the hon. member for Saskatoon on a very well prepared and well delivered speech this afternoon. I welcome this opportunity to join with my colleagues who have taken this opportunity as the first which has been presented to discuss the estimates of a very important department, one of the largest spending departments in this great business of government where we are at the present time spending almost $7 billion.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Where did you get that figure from?
I should like to reiterate the criticism which has been made by some of my colleagues in connection with the haphazard, shilly-shally way in which the business of the house has been handled.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Would the hon. member advise me where he gets the figure of $7 billion for the department of health and welfare?

That is $7 billion total government spending. The hon. lady probably has the estimates before her, which amount to some $6,700 million, but with all the supplementary estimates this figure will probably go up to $7 billion.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I understood him to refer to my department.

The hon. lady misunderstood my remarks. It is rather interesting to notice how properly trained "seals" on the back benches are following the advice given to them by the "old gang" sitting in the front benches and not participating in this debate. No doubt they have some ideas too on how the department of health

and welfare might be improved in areas where there is greater need for work and research. Although my experience in this house does not extend as far back as some others, it has always been the rule that a short time after the preliminary debates in each session take place, motions of supply are presented, and following that two days of every week are set aside for the discussion of the estimates of different departments. This practice has not been followed in this session, so therefore we as a responsible opposition must seize this opportunity to bring before the government areas in regard to action in which we feel they have been delinquent. It is also interesting to note that the parties to my left, which are always the proponents of social welfare schemes, have not deemed it worth while to participate in this debate at any time during the last two days or to make any comments on this very important department.
Although for many years medical organizations, individually and collectively, have been issuing warnings as to the hazards of cigarette smoking, it was not until the announcement made by the United States department of health some months ago that the matter seemed to be brought to a head. In fact, it almost amounted in some cases to a national hysteria. We all remember the reactions which followed when through our news media- radio, t.v. and the newspapers

the effects of this hazard were made known. I might join the hon. member for Simcoe East in congratulating the minister on her ability to stop smoking as she did. However, the notoriety given to this action and the fact that a fund of $600,000 was set up for research into the subject sent the hon. member for Norfolk into such a political "tizzy" that his pleas to the Minister of Agriculture could no longer be denied. In spite of the fact that there were many more pressing subjects of a national nature which should have been discussed in the standing committee on agriculture, all of the meetings of that committee so far this year have been taken up with a discussion of ways and means to increase production of tobacco.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, on the one hand we find the government has set up a fund to examine and report on the effects on the health of the nation of the use of tobacco; and on the other, before the report is presented, we find another area crying for assistance to produce more of this product. This is not only a national but an international problem, we realize, because of the report that
Interim Supply
was issued by the United States; but I was rather interested the other day in picking up one of the Soviet magazines which are sent to most members of the house and noticing in it an article on cigarette smoking. I do not often read these publications but this was quite an interesting article. Apparently Russian scientists were unable to prove that the use of tobacco was a direct cause of lung cancer, but they found that its use did increase the activity of the disease and tended to cause a reduction in the efficiency of the respiratory organs. In fact, according to the article they were so perturbed about the situation that they have entered upon a comprehensive program of education in their schools to teach children about the hazards of this easy to acquire and hard to kick habit. I think it would be well if at some of the dominion-provincial conferences between the Minister of National Health and Welfare and her colleagues in the provincial governments some consideration were given to a program of this type in Canada.
However, Mr. Chairman, the use of tobacco and its effects is not the main theme of my remarks tonight. I should like to discuss a subject that is closely related, a subject that scientific research has proved has a great deal to do with causing cancer, throat and lung infections and sometimes heart disease. I refer to air pollution. It is my sincere hope that through this discussion I may bring once again to the attention of the house and the nation in general an awareness of the dangers we encounter in the air we breathe. This is not a new subject for discussion in the house. I remember that in 1956 the former member for Brant-Haldimand presented a private member's bill the theme of which was air pollution and its hazards to health.
That this is a constant threat to our health is borne out by the many editorial and newspaper articles written on the subject. It was brought home rather forcefully in my own area during the recent Lions club convention held in Kitchener. I should like to quote from an article in the London Free Press of Tuesday, June 2, 1964. The article is headed, "Blame Parade 'Poison' On Monoxide Fumes", and reads in part as follows:
Four members of the Georgina township police band and majorette corps were released from St. Mary's general hospital here yesterday after spending the night in hospital with possible carbon monoxide poisoning following the Lions club parade Sunday.
Dr. G. E. (Duff) Wilson, Kitchener's medical officer of health, said that food poisoning has been ruled out. Of the four patients interviewed, two had not eaten in the area and the other two

Interim Supply
had eaten different things. Twelve members of the band and majorettes were taken to hospitals following the parade.
Dr. Wilson said last night that the band members were marching behind a motorized float giving off carbon monoxide fumes during the 21 mile parade. "This could easily be the cause", he said.
This identical situation is happening practically every day and every week, particularly during the summer, in towns, cities and villages all across Canada.
Canadians have fought hard for the pure food laws and Canadian manufacturers spend millions of dollars each year to guarantee that our food is uncontaminated. We have as a government introduced legislation to assist municipalities to provide adequate water and sewage systems and have made available millions of dollars to carry out these plans. There have been many debates on the question of fluoridation to prevent tooth decay but it was not until 1956, according to the answer to my question 1,065 of this session, that anything was done in a national way about the air we breathe. I quote from the return:
The air pollution program was initiated in 1956 within the occupational health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare and has cost about $400,000 since that time. The program is closely integrated with air pollution control activities of provincial health departments.
This return would indicate that control matters do come under provincial jurisdiction, and after the debate of last week on student loans, when the bogey of interference in educational matters was raised, I wonder whether it might not come into this matter too. However the health of the nation is important to all levels of government. This is a national problem. I do not feel that the amount of $50,000 a year is adequate to deal with this very complex and difficult problem. It would appear that our neighbours to the south are very conscious of the problem and are so disturbed that they are doing something about it. I have here a recent newspaper report headed, "Senate Rebuffs Lobbies, Passes Air Pollution Bill", which reads in part as follows:
Despite bitter opposition by big business lobbies, the U.S. Senate passed a bill authorizing a $182 million, five year program of federal aid to state and local governments in combatting air pollution.
Senator Edmund S. Muskie, chief sponsor of the bill, explained that its main provisions would help "initiate and improve air pollution control programs, expand research, and give the U.S. health, education and welfare department enforcement power in interstate air pollution cases."
Apparently the bill was opposed by the national association of manufacturers who

tried to intimate that once again this was an encroachment on state rights. However Senator Muskie pointed out that few states have any laws on the subject and still fewer states and cities are doing a real enforcement job. Then he went on to say:
Fresh air is life. Polluted air means disease and death. Untold thousands of Americans have suffered and died as a result of the effects of air pollution.
Another senator who supported the bill had this to say:
Now it is clear that additional government authority and action are necessary to assure the right to breathe pure air.
The question of air pollution was brought into world wide prominence a few years ago. We all remember the situation that developed in Los Angeles and which lasted for many months. To a large extent it was due to the fact that Los Angeles has more automobiles for its population than any other city in the world. I should like to quote from an article that appeared in the Canadian Weekly published by the Toronto Star, for the week of November 23, 1963. The article is by John O'Keefe. We sometimes say these things cannot happen to us, but the article reads in part as follows:
During the early hours of Tuesday, Sept. 9, 1952, a light haze developed over the Windsor-Detroit area and it got worse as the day wore on. By early evening people began coughing and eyes watered in the acrid air. Two days later the smog hung like a thick blanket over the area and visibility was so bad that two ships ran aground in the Detroit river. Traffic crawled and tempers flared as people became more irritable. Plants withered and died in the murky atmosphere and doctors were overrun with complaints of chest troubles, nausea and diarrhea.
The smog lasted three days and during that time at least 35 infants died-twice the normal number for the period-and the number of people dying of respiratory diseases jumped two and a half times.
This happened in Windsor, Ontario in 1952. However, Mr. Chairman, as has been proven on so many occasions, there is another type of smog that has only recently been discovered. It is an invisible smog which the sun brews from the unseen chemicals and gases that remain suspended in the air, too fine to be seen except with complicated equipment. This is ozone which is created through a photochemical reaction of the hydrocarbon and oxides of nitrogen discharged from automobile exhausts and diesel engines. Add to this the deadly carbon monoxide fumes which are being spewed into the atmosphere by the ever increasing number of motor vehicles, and you have a doubly dangerous situation.

You can neither taste, smell nor feel carbon
monoxide, yet in a very short time it can be the means of impairing the mental faculties of a driver to the point where co-ordination of muscles and the ability to react properly in the operation of a motor vehicle are below even the minimum requirements of safety.
There have been, as I indicated earlier in my speech, many articles written. Statistics have been provided by most eminent authorities, all of which indicate that this is, as the article indicates, a silent killer. According to the return I mentioned previously, it would appear we are depending on our neighbour to the south for most of our information and our research on this subject. This is rather interesting, Mr. Chairman, when we realize that we are only spending approximately $50,000 a year in this most important field of research. This is what the return I received from the minister says:
Intensive studies on various control systems have been under way in the United States by the public health service, the state of California, the automobile manufacturers association in Detroit and other organizations for some years. These systems include the design of new engine processes, improved carburetor design and a catalytic or flame combustion of exhaust gas by means of an afterburner. The state of California has established performance requirements for the control of contaminants in exhaust of motor vehicles but no system has been improved for installation as yet. The Department of National Health and Welfare is keeping abreast of such developments.
A partial palliative has been found in the installation of a crankcase control device to prevent air pollution from engine blowby gas. This device is now manufactured for installation in the United States.
This is not good enough, Mr. Chairman, for a nation like Canada. We spend, in a federal way, over $400 million on a hospital program and yet we spent only $50,000 a year in the last eight years to protect our citizens from this menace. One of our own doctors in the department of health and welfare has this to say, as reported in this article:
Dr. Morris Katz, as air pollution consultant to the federal government, estimates that the minimum amount of money needed for air pollution research in Canada is $18 million a year, spread among federal, provincial and local organizations. "And that," he adds, "would be for a fairly moderate show."
The report I received from the minister indicates they have discovered a device to reduce or alleviate the injurious gases given off by automobiles. I should like to get back now to the question of Indian hospitals. There has been a tendency lately to change over from the hospitals on a reserve to hospitals in adjoining cities and towns. The reason for this, of course, may be twofold. It is either a financial reason, or possibly because more facilities can be provided in the larger centres. Be that as it may, I should like to point out that there are other factors to be considered. Some reserves cover hundreds of square miles. Transportation is not always available on these reserves, especially when there are adverse weather conditions. These people may have automobiles, but they do not always work when the weather is cold or when it is raining to excess, or for other reasons. When the hospital is on the reserve, however, these people can sometimes reach the hospital in cases of emergency by using a team of horses. Some of them in certain areas still have horses. However, they could not be expected to take horses or tractors out on the highway.
I have in mind my own area in central Alberta, for example. I am sure there are similar situations elsewhere in Canada on the reserves. I refer specifically to the Indians at Hobbema. They have their own hospital. Most of them have told me personally that they were quite satisfied with it. I have never heard any of them say they were not. When a new hospital was built at the nearby city of Wetaskiwin, a third storey was added, ostensibly to take care of the Indian patients from Hobbema. The Indians have told me also in no uncertain terms that they prefer their own hospital. They do not mind my saying that they do not feel at home anywhere else. They say they are not in the same financial category as other patients in a hospital, and therefore they are embarrassed by the fact they are not as well dressed as other visitors to the hospital. It is sometimes quite a strain on these people who come from so far, as they also feel they are not well dressed.
At present the hospital at Hobbema, the one that used to serve the Indian population, is being operated as a health clinic for less serious cases. Perhaps this is meant to be on a temporary basis and I would strongly urge that, at least, this would be continued.
